items.titleTR: How the emojis and fashion choices of Germany’s far-right supporters get around the ban on Nazi symbolism

slots.packetSpot:
The AfD’s rise in state elections in Germany has reignited debate over the far right’s political weight. Cas Mudde stresses that the party, which received 43.8 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt and 38.2 percent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, did not reach the absolute majority needed to govern alone; in Berlin, meanwhile, the Left Party came first. According to Mudde, dissatisfaction with established parties is directed not only to the right but also to the left; the risk posed by the far right to liberal democracy should not be equated with parties referred to as the “far left.”

The possibility of changes in state governments has also sparked a political and institutional debate over the sharing of classified information. Some politicians and security officials have voiced concern that information could leak to Russia or to groups under investigation on suspicion of links to organised crime in states governed by the AfD or the Left Party. The AfD rejects accusations that it is effectively allied with Vladimir Putin; the Left Party also does not accept claims linking it to organised crime and antisemitism.

Under strict bans on Nazi symbols, some circles associated with the far right are alleged to use more covert signs through Norse and Viking imagery, clothing brands and emojis. However, it is specifically noted that a rune, emoji or brand alone is not proof of political affiliation, and that the meaning of these signs varies according to context.
slots.packetTitle: The far right's visibility threshold

items.descriptionTR: Roelf Meyer tells the BBC that being a white Afrikaner gives him legitimacy to challenge Trump's claim of a genocide.
items.titleTR: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC

items.descriptionTR: South Africa’s problems with crime, racial rhetoric, land reform, economic empowerment and foreign policy are serious. They do not add up to ‘white genocide’.
items.titleTR: Letter to US ambassador Bozell — Afrikaners are being used as a political football

slots.packetSpot:
Donald Trump’s claim, raised in political debates and diplomatic engagements in the United States, that white Afrikaners in South Africa are being subjected to genocide is rejected by South African officials and others. Ambassador to Washington Roelf Meyer, stressing that he is himself an Afrikaner, says the reality of violence and crime in the country is being misrepresented.

While violence on farms and overall crime rates remain a serious issue, most victims of crime are Black, according to police data. Expert views cited indicate that this picture cannot be described as persecution. Tensions surrounding crime, racist rhetoric, land reform, economic empowerment and foreign policy persist; whether these amount to a claim of “white genocide” remains the fundamental point of division between the US administration and opposing voices in South Africa.
slots.packetTitle: The shadow cast by a “white genocide” claim

items.descriptionTR: The TPLF advanced toward Afdeera after taking Erebti, with at least 150,000 people feared displaced in Afar alone. The offensive targets the Djibouti corridor, through which almost all of Ethiopia's international trade flows, giving the rebels potential leverage over the federal government.
items.titleTR: Tigray rebels push into Afar as Ethiopia blames neighbours

items.descriptionTR: Addis Ababa has accused Sudan and Eritrea of backing armed groups fighting its federal forces in the north, claims Khartoum has rejected as renewed clashes raise fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
items.titleTR: Ethiopia accuses Sudan, Eritrea of backing Tigray forces as fighting escalates

items.descriptionTR:
Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.
About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.
items.titleTR: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war

items.descriptionTR: A resident of Mekelle says the city is calm but people are stressed after the outbreak of fighting in the region.
items.titleTR: Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates, resident tells BBC

items.descriptionTR: Sept 28 - Ethiopia's military and allied militiamen captured the strategic town of Alamata south of Tigray's capital, a pro-government militia said on Monday, turning the tables after an opposition offensive launched from the region last week.
items.titleTR: Ethiopian pro-government forces claim capture of strategic Tigray town

slots.packetSpot:
Heavy fighting between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces has reportedly resumed, spreading beyond Tigray into Afar and Amhara. While the sides claim that the other started the latest escalation, the TPLF says it is defending itself against an attack by the federal government; the government, meanwhile, alleges that Tigray forces launched the initial attack after seizing airports.

In Afar, Erebti is reported to have fallen into the hands of TPLF forces, with an advance towards Afdeera also reported, while an estimate that at least 150,000 people have been displaced is being shared with the caveat that no definitive figure could be given. A claim that Alamata in southern Tigray was captured by pro-government forces has not been independently verified. Disruptions to telephone and internet networks continue in Tigray; cash shortages, panic buying, and difficulties accessing food and medicine are reported in Mekelle. No casualties were initially reported in a drone strike on the Tigrai TV headquarters.

An alliance formed by the TPLF with six other armed groups that have declared their aim to remove Abiy Ahmed’s government from office broadens the political ground of the conflict. Ethiopia’s army commander accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting armed groups; Sudan rejected the allegations as baseless, while Eritrea and Egypt did not respond publicly in the statements reported. The United Nations and the African Union said they were concerned by reports of harm to civilians and the use of drones, calling for the fighting to stop and for a return to talks within the framework of the Pretoria Agreement.

About 600,000 people were killed in the 2020-2022 war, according to African Union estimates. The 2022 Pretoria Agreement ended large-scale fighting, but unresolved issues had kept tensions alive.
slots.packetTitle: A widening war front in Tigray

items.descriptionTR: The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and have since been launching increasing attacks on Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East.
items.titleTR: Saudi coalition says it intercepted Houthi drones and missiles bound for Saudi Arabia

items.descriptionTR:
Schools in Riyadh have told parents that classes will move online for the rest of the week, in an abrupt change that has not been explained by the Saudi authorities.
Several schools in the Saudi capital sent messages to parents on Saturday saying lessons would be held remotely from Sunday to Thursday. The National has seen at least three such messages from three different schools.
None gave a reason for the decision. There has been no official announcement of a formal measure covering schools across the city and the Ministry of Education has not commented publicly.
The shift comes at a tense time for the kingdom. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said early on Saturday that its air defences had intercepted and destroyed two drones launched by the Houthis towards the Riyadh area.
Coalition spokesman Brig Gen Turki Al Malki said two ballistic missiles fired towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait were also brought down.
Two days earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and the Red Sea port area of Yanbu. The Iran-backed rebels have stepped up their near-daily attacks on Saudi Arabia since July, when they declared a naval blockade on the kingdom.
Hours before Saturday's interceptions, the military chiefs of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met in Riyadh to discuss threats facing the kingdom. The three countries signed a joint defence pact last month under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.
Riyadh is also entering a busy week of events, with traffic expected to be particularly heavy.
Saudi Arabia has used its Madrasati online platform to move classes out of school buildings before, most recently for a day in Riyadh and the Eastern Province in December.
items.titleTR: Riyadh schools switch to remote learning amid Houthi threat

slots.packetSpot:
Brigadier General Turki Al Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi Arabia-led coalition, said air defences had intercepted two Houthi drones launched toward Riyadh and two ballistic missiles targeting Khamis Mushait. The coalition had also reported two days earlier that six ballistic missiles heading toward Taif and the Yanbu port area on the Red Sea coast had been intercepted.

At least three schools in Riyadh informed parents that classes would be held online from Sunday through Thursday. No reason was given for the decision; the Education Ministry also made no public statement, and no official citywide measure was announced.

The Houthis had declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, then stepped up their attacks on Saudi cities and maritime shipping. According to the United Nations, more than 122,000 people were displaced as the conflict in Yemen escalated; 674 people were killed and 2,998 injured between August 6 and September 18.
slots.packetTitle: Remote learning under Riyadh's shadow of threat

items.titleTR: Russia strikes Ukraine as Putin denies plans to attack Europe amid growing tensions

items.descriptionTR: KYIV, Sept 28 - Ukraine's military has recaptured more territory from Russian forces in the north of the Donetsk region, a senior military commander said on Monday, in an operation aimed at complicating Moscow's assault on Ukraine's key eastern strongholds.
items.titleTR: Ukrainian forces advance in key eastern battlefield, senior commander says

items.descriptionTR:
￼
If you do not follow the Twitter feed of the Ukrainian Third Army Corps, you should. It does not tweet a great deal, but when it does, especially recently, it has been fascinating. For those of you who do not know of it, the Third Corps is one of the best units in the Ukrainian military
items.titleTR: For Ukraine, some good news but also some bad news

items.descriptionTR:
In recent weeks, Ukrainian drones have targeted large warehouses across Russia, destroying millions of dollars of merchandise stored inside them.
These warehouses and logistics hubs belong to Wildberries, the Russian equivalent to Amazon.  Ukraine is taking aim at Ozon, Russia’s second-largest online retailer, too.
Ukraine says it’s targeting these companies because they’ve been providing supplies to soldiers on the front line.
But according to Matthew Sussex, associate professor in strategic studies at Deakin University in Australia, who talked to The Conversation Weekly podcast, Kyiv’s strategy also intends to disrupt the lives of everyday Russians.
When you put in an online order that can’t go through because the merchandise has been blown up by Ukrainian drones, that starts to put indirect political pressure on people like Vladimir Putin because it hits the everyday Russian consumer.
But as the war drags on well into its fourth year, is there anything that could put pressure on Putin to withdraw troops from Ukraine?
[Putin] has given no sign that he wants an off ramp. But the pressures that will build on him to seek one will continue to grow.
He really has staked his legacy on this invasion of Ukraine. And that’s something that would be really hard for him personally to back away from, in terms of his political longevity and his place in Russia’s history books.

￼ Ukraine wants to disrupt the convenience of 21st century life for Russians. Will it be effective in ending the war?
items.titleTR: How Ukraine is bringing the war home to Russia

slots.packetSpot:
The war is expanding beyond the front line. While cities, homes, infrastructure and commercial logistics targets in Ukraine bear the impact of Russian attacks, Ukraine’s reported territorial gains in Donetsk and Ukrainian drone strikes on commercial logistics facilities inside Russia show that the conflict has also drawn supply networks and the functioning of daily life into the battlefield.

The casualties and damage reported by local officials, together with the number of drones that the Ukrainian air force said were used in overnight attacks, reveal the scale of pressure on cities. Figures for gains in the Vivaldi operation in Donetsk were announced by Ukrainian commander Andrii Biletskyi, while differing assessments exist over the extent of activity around Lyman.

The targeting of warehouses linked to Wildberries and Ozon in Russia is based on Ukraine’s statement that these facilities supply soldiers at the front. According to Matthew Sussex, the attacks may also reflect an effort to exert indirect pressure on the Kremlin by disrupting the daily lives of Russian consumers. Vladimir Putin’s remarks that they are not preparing for conflict with Europe, meanwhile, do not dispel security concerns in Europe.
slots.packetTitle: The war’s lengthening line

items.descriptionTR: No casualties were reported after a Russian drone struck a train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials left the area.
items.titleTR: Watch: Why a Russian strike on train near Ukraine-Poland border could mark an escalation

items.descriptionTR:
Drohnen und Raketen, die nah an der polnischen Grenze einschlagen - der Krieg gegen die Ukraine rückt spürbar an den Alltag der Menschen heran. Schutzräume und Warn-SMS gewinnen an Bedeutung. Wie ist die Stimmung vor Ort? Von P. Milling.

items.titleTR: Polen: Wenn der Krieg näher kommt

slots.packetSpot:
The war in Ukraine is becoming a more visible part of everyday life in Poland’s border regions. A Russian drone reportedly struck a train near the Ukrainian-Polish border, with no casualties reported; Boris Johnson and senior European officials were said to have left the area shortly before.

Residents of Lubelskie and Podkarpackie are reportedly frequently sent warning messages, and sirens are said to sound. In Lublin, a school evacuated around 550 students, teachers and staff during an alarm; the headteacher said the decision had been accused by some of causing panic.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk, based on intelligence assessments, warned countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, about possible hybrid drone and missile attacks that could target them. According to officials’ statements, air defences have been strengthened, additional units have been deployed to border crossings and new Patriot systems have been stationed. Lubelskie is reported to have 3,500 shelters for around two million people, with more than half a billion zlotys invested in civil protection over the past two years; in rural areas, however, the nearest shelter is said to be dozens of kilometres away.
slots.packetTitle: War draws closer from beyond the border

items.descriptionTR:
￼
European military experts warn that Russia is actively planning targeted aggression against NATO to test alliance solidarity. Recent high-alert incidents include a foiled explosive drone plot at a German airport and a strike near the Ukraine-Poland border targeting European VIPs. However, officials are deeply split on the immediacy of a conventional threat.
items.titleTR: Putin appears to be eyeing NATO. The question is, will he actually attack?

items.descriptionTR: The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said on Thursday that the risk of Russian military action against Nato countries was growing and an outright invasion was "highly unlikely" but possible.
items.titleTR: Danish spy agency: Russian invasion of Nato country 'highly unlikely' but cannot be ruled out

slots.packetSpot:
Intelligence and security circles in Europe are divided in their assessment that the risk of possible Russian military moves against NATO countries has increased, while the prospect of an imminent and overt invasion has not become certain. Thomas Ahrenkiel, head of the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, described the risk of a limited attack on one or several NATO countries bordering Russia as low but rising; while considering the occupation of a NATO country very unlikely, he did not rule it out entirely.

The DDIS expects an intensification of hybrid activities, including sabotage aimed at disrupting support for Ukraine, actions targeting defence companies or railway lines carrying military equipment, and destructive cyberattacks that could paralyse critical societal functions. According to the agency, a limited military move could arise in the coming months; by contrast, a military buildup would take months and would be difficult to conceal. Ahrenkiel also stressed that they do not expect a conventional Russian attack on Denmark.

Other assessments suggest that Russia may be actively planning some form of aggression, while whether this has been decided upon and how imminent it is remain disputed. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned that a major development could occur this year; Tarmo Miilits, a senior official at Estonia’s Interior Ministry, said they had seen no indication that Russia intends a military attack on any NATO ally. Finnish President Alexander Stubb also called for avoiding alarmist language.

Germany held Putin responsible for what was described as a drone incident targeting Leipzig Airport. Polish officials said they strongly suspect Kremlin agents were behind an arson attack at a satellite communications ground station providing a critical link with the Ukrainian armed forces. Russia confirmed Ukraine’s attack on a passenger train near the Polish border while denying the allegation that it had attempted to assassinate European diplomats; Putin also rejected accusations of aggression and blamed NATO.

Another threshold in the debate is NATO’s Article 5: the principle that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all members. When hybrid actions would cross that threshold, and how the alliance would respond, remain unclear.
slots.packetTitle: An uncertain threshold at NATO’s border

A 23-year-old woman was shot dead during an alleged robbery on her way to work in Temong Section, Tembisa, amid heightened community concerns over women's safety in Ekurhuleni.
A 23-year-old woman was shot dead during an alleged robbery on her way to work in Temong Section, Tembisa, amid heightened community concerns over women's safety in Ekurhuleni.
items.titleTR: 23-year-old woman shot dead on her way to work in Tembisa

items.descriptionTR: The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".
items.titleTR: 'Enough is enough': Women protest after string of murders near Johannesburg

items.descriptionTR: South African police say that another woman's body has been discovered in the Ekurhuleni area east of Johannesburg
items.titleTR: 11th woman's body in South Africa as authorities investigate recent spate of killings

slots.packetSpot:
In Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, the killing of women and the discovery of their bodies since July have intensified the police investigation, fear and anger. The number and scope of cases have been reported with varying information at different times; police have not yet confirmed any common link between the incidents or the possibility of a serial killer.

In the Temong area of Tembisa, a 23-year-old woman was shot dead on Monday morning while on her way to work. Gauteng police are investigating murder and robbery, stating that her belongings were taken; they said there is no confirmed link between this attack and the other cases, and that no one has been detained.

Bodies have been found at different locations across Ekurhuleni, including Tembisa, Springs and Kempton Park. A suspect was detained in connection with the murder of Ntombifuthu Nxumalo; it was reported that a 36-year-old suspect was arrested in another case, while two women appeared in court in connection with another murder. As relatives of Dineo Motapane and Itumeleng described their disappearances, protests in Kempton Park brought calls for stronger measures against violence against women to the fore.

The South African Human Rights Commission announced that 569 women were killed between April and June. Amnesty International called for femicide to be recognised as a separate crime, while President Cyril Ramaphosa pledged that the crimes in Ekurhuleni would be investigated.
slots.packetTitle: Alarm over women's safety in Ekurhuleni

items.descriptionTR: Manchester City are refusing to concede defeat despite reports that they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 Premier League financial trangressions the club allegedly committed between 2009 and 2018.
items.titleTR: OWN GOAL: Manchester City’s future in the air after reports of Premier League guilty verdict

items.descriptionTR: Football finance expert Kieran Maguire says the potential sanctions for Manchester City will be 'significant' after the sources told BBC Sport that the club has been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.
items.titleTR: What could the potential sanctions for Man City be?

items.descriptionTR:
One of the biggest cheating scandals in world sports history has erupted in England: Manchester City has reportedly been found guilty of 114 of the 115 alleged breaches of English Premier League financial rules brought against the club in 2023.
The charges relate to the club’s incredibly successful spell between 2009 and 2018 when they won seven major titles, headlined by three Premier League championships.
Manchester City was bought in 2008 by the Abu Dhabi United Group, led by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan – a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family.
The group now owns or has a stake in 13 football teams across the world, from New York to Melbourne, meaning there may be ramifications well beyond England.
But Manchester City is expected to appeal, having long protested its innocence – so this case is not over yet.
What are the charges?
The guilty findings are a potentially seismic development in a case that has hung over English football for more than three years.
The charges cover several areas, including:
	•	the accuracy of financial information supplied to the Premier League
	•	player and manager remuneration
	•	compliance with Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) and Premier League financial regulations
	•	cooperation with the league’s investigation.
But there are important caveats. The independent commission’s decision has not yet been published, no sanction has been announced, Manchester City has consistently denied wrongdoing – which is why an appeal is expected.
Until the written decision is available, any assessment of precisely what City did and what should happen next would be premature.
What could happen to Manchester City?
Recent Premier League cases demonstrate how breaches of financial rules can result in sporting sanctions.
In recent years, Everton was initially deducted ten points (reduced to six points on appeal) for breaching the league’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules, while Nottingham Forest was deducted four points. Both sides narrowly avoided relegation after the sanctions.
But these cases provide limited guidance for Manchester City. They concerned relatively discrete breaches of spending rules, whereas the charges against City cover multiple categories of alleged misconduct over almost a decade.
So any attempt to extrapolate a likely points deduction for City from Everton or Forest would be speculative.
More severe possibilities – including relegation or expulsion from the Premier League – have inevitably been discussed, as has the prospect of retrospectively stripping City of titles.
Little precedent exists for the latter in English professional team sport. Saracens were relegated from rugby union’s Premiership following salary-cap breaches in 2020, but their previously won titles were not removed.
Australian sport, however, provides precedent. The National Rugby League (NRL) stripped the Melbourne Storm of their 2007 and 2009 premierships, three minor premierships, and all their 2010 competition points after it uncovered systematic salary cap breaches.
Those cases illustrate possible sporting sanctions. But they cannot establish what City’s penalty should be before the commission publishes its reasoning.
Could the consequences spread beyond Manchester?
The shockwaves from this case could also spread overseas.
The City Football Group owns or has a stake in 13 clubs worldwide – including Melbourne City, New York City and Italy’s Palermo.
For example, Melbourne City joined City Football Group in 2014 and is now wholly owned by it.
A Premier League sanction against the English team would not automatically apply to the Melbourne club.
Yet if the published findings concern governance, financial reporting or transactions within the wider ownership structure, they may prompt scrutiny of how the group oversees its international clubs.
That would not establish wrongdoing at Melbourne City or any other City Football Group club. It would test whether rules and oversight built around individual clubs adequately address shared ownership and decision-making across borders.
Beyond any official Premier League sanctions, there could be more ramifications. Many rival Premier League sides are reportedly considering legal action for compensation, claiming they have been impacted by City’s alleged cheating.
Winning Premier League titles, qualifying for and winning major European championships can earn clubs hundreds of millions of dollars.
But a league penalty and a compensation claim are separate matters.
No rival club is automatically entitled to compensation. Each would need to show a proven breach caused a measurable loss, despite the many results and decisions that shape a season.
Why this is far from over
Whatever sanction ultimately follows, the dispute is unlikely to end there. Manchester City are expected to appeal the commission’s findings, meaning any final resolution could still be some way off.
A successful appeal could substantially alter, or even overturn, the significance of the initial ruling. Until that process is exhausted, both the findings and their consequences should therefore be treated as unresolved.
The case reaches beyond football. The Financial Times has described the verdict as the latest test of United Kingdom–United Arab Emirates relations, with the British government seeking closer economic ties with the UAE and greater investment from Abu Dhabi.
These wider political and economic considerations illustrate how the ownership of modern football clubs can intersect with international investment, politics and diplomacy.
The commission’s full decision remains unpublished. Until its reasons and any sanction are known, we cannot say which of these consequences will follow.
The case already asks a broader question: can football’s rules keep pace with the financial and governance structures that now connect clubs across leagues and countries?

Manchester City could be facing enormous sanctions for cheating – and the fallout may spread to its 13 teams around the world, from New York to Melbourne.
items.titleTR: Stripped titles? Compensating rivals? How the Manchester City cheating scandal could play out

items.descriptionTR:
Friday’s verdict against Manchester City will change everything we understood about their Premier League title triumphs
Welcome, then, to the age of asterisk. Whatever punishment Manchester City and their owners receive at the end of this process, the fact remains, everything is tainted now.
Overturn the tables, scatter the gold coins. Throw your medals in the bin. You cheated to win them. Whatever that thing was, it’s done. Stolen glory, stolen income, stolen joy. Every chant, every “we won the lot”, every awkward documentary scene about the deep, throbbing heart of this empire of love. It all looks odd, sinister, cold, sloppy, but also, and this is always the best response, utterly absurd.
items.titleTR: The age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted now | Barney Ronay

slots.packetSpot:
As findings alleging that Manchester City breached financial rules during the 2009-2018 period were reported, the club is said to have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges. The Premier League has not publicly confirmed the decision; the independent commission's reasoned ruling and any possible sanction have not yet been published. City, which has long denied the charges, is expected to appeal.

The allegations cover the accuracy of financial information submitted to the Premier League, player and manager payments, compliance with Premier League and UEFA financial regulations, and cooperation with the investigation. Although possibilities such as a fine, points deduction, relegation or expulsion are being discussed, it remains unclear which sanction will be imposed.

Everton and Nottingham Forest having received points deductions over financial rules is cited as a precedent; however, the scope and duration of the charges brought against City cannot be directly compared with these examples. The status of past championships and possible compensation claims by rival clubs are also on the agenda, but none of these has been finalised. The fact that Abu Dhabi United Group acquired Manchester City in 2008 and that City Football Group has ownership or partnership stakes in 13 clubs worldwide has led to assessments that the matter could extend to governance and oversight debates beyond England; no breach has been identified involving affiliated clubs.
slots.packetTitle: An asterisk over Manchester City's era of success

items.descriptionTR: Watch highlights as Warrington Wolves earn a thrilling narrow Super League semi-final win over Leeds Rhinos to reach their first Grand Final for eight years.
items.titleTR: Warrington reach Grand Final with Leeds win

items.descriptionTR: Ahead of the Super League Grand Final between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity, on Saturday October 3 at Old Trafford, we take you through everything you need to know...
items.titleTR: Super League Grand Final 2026: Everything you need to know

slots.packetSpot:
Warrington Wolves' narrow semi-final victory over Leeds Rhinos has taken the team to the Super League Grand Final for the first time in eight years. Following Wakefield Trinity's semi-final win over Wigan, the two teams will meet at Old Trafford on Saturday, 3 October; kick-off is at 18:00, with Sky Sports coverage beginning at 17:00.

Warrington and Wakefield, who finished third and fourth respectively in the 2026 league table, have no Grand Final titles. Warrington last played in the final in 2018, while Wakefield will reach this stage for the first time. Warrington won one of their two meetings during the season 27-16, while Wakefield won the other 25-18; pre-match assessments therefore see both sides as having a clear chance of winning.
slots.packetTitle: A new final at Old Trafford

items.descriptionTR:
The Knights’ incredible preliminary final win over the Penrith Panthers showcased everything Justin Holbrook has done to turn the club around
Few teams have been mired in mediocrity longer than the Newcastle Knights, a club from a region that few dispute is the heartland of rugby league in Australia. They are built on the legend of Andrew “Joey” Johns and Paul “Chief” Harragon and so many others but have, for the better part of the last quarter-century, been an irrelevance.
No more. After one of the most compelling, controversial and climactic preliminary finals in the history of the game, the Knights are on their way to the 2026 NRL grand final just 12 months after claiming their fourth wooden spoon in 11 seasons. Hollywood’s finest scriptwriter could not have written the story of Newcastle’s rise over the last year – and even the most creative could not have put together what will live in folklore as one of the most dramatic grand final qualifiers the game has seen.
items.titleTR: Newcastle find themselves the NRL’s fairytale team after scarcely believable return to glory | Nick Tedeschi

slots.packetSpot:
The Newcastle Knights defeated the Penrith Panthers 22-14 to reach the men's NRL grand final for the first time since 2001. The team, which played the second half with 12 men after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip-drop tackle, will face the Sydney Roosters.

Penrith playmaker Nathan Cleary reportedly suffered a serious leg injury, while some other Panthers players were also injured. Justin Holbrook said the support of fans in Newcastle and the Hunter region gave the team strength; for the Knights, who finished last season at the bottom of the table, the result stands out as a remarkable turnaround.
slots.packetTitle: Newcastle's return from a long night

Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons relationship appears to be getting worse.
The Jalen Duren contract situation with the Detroit Pistons isn’t improving. In fact, it’s getting worse.
According to ESPN’s Shams Charania, Pistons center Jalen Duren won’t attend the Pistons’ media day on Monday and isn’t expected to be there for the start of training camp.
MORE:Jalen Duren could force his way out of Detroit amid contract dispute
This follows his rejection of the Pistons’ five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed offer in restricted free agency. Thursday’s deadline includes a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer, but it’s unclear whether it will get that far.
Duren was fantastic for the Pistons last season, averaging 19.5 points, 10.5 rebounds, and two assists per game. This was his fourth NBA season, and it was his best by far.
What’s next for Jalen Duren and the Pistons?
￼
Jan 27, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Detroit Pistons guard Cade Cunningham (2) and center Jalen Duren (0) react to a foul called in the first quarter against the Denver Nuggets at Ball Arena. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images
Duren has been away from the Pistons for most of the offseason, and that doesn’t appear to be changing. Teams could also try to trade for him if this saga continues into the preseason and even the regular season.
The Pistons made the NBA Playoffs last season before losing to the Cleveland Cavaliers in the second round. They beat the Orlando Magic in the first round.
This was the second straight season in which the Pistons made the playoffs. Let’s see if they can make it three in a row this year.

items.descriptionTR:
The Miami Dolphins could be in the market for a free agent running back after a season-ending injury to De’Von Achane.
￼
LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - JANUARY 04: Kareem Hunt #29 of the Kansas City Chiefs warms up before the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The Raiders defeated the Kansas City Chiefs 14-12. (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images
The Miami Dolphins lost running back De’Von Achane to a torn ACL on Sunday, ending the season for the team’s top rusher and a 2025 Pro Bowl selection. Miami currently has two running backs, Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II, on the 53-man roster, with Jarquez Hunter and Carlos Washington, Jr., on the practice squad. Miami could look to move forward with that group, but they could also look to add a veteran free agent. But who is available?
Miami is not going to break the bank to sign someone, but they could look to add a veteran on a minimum deal, making sure they have the depth needed to get through the season. The Dolphins’ running game is the focal point of the offensive system, and they are going to need increased depth at the position without Achane.
Kareem Hunt
The former Kansas City Chiefs running back was a Pro Bowl selection in 2017 as a rookie when he led the league in rushing yards. He finished last year with 163 carriers for 611 yards and eight touchdowns. He is not a direct replacement for Achane, but could provide another power option with Gordon, serving as a compliment to Wright’s speed.
He would not be a workload carrying running back at this point in his career, but he could be a good veteran rotation guy who can handle 10 carries a game.
Raheem Mostert
Could Miami bring back former Dolphins runner Mostert to solidify the group? Mostert has bounced around the league throughout much of his career, but had extended periods with the San Francisco 49ers (2016-2021) and Miami (2022-2024). He was selected to the Pro Bowl in 2023 when he led the league in rushing touchdowns with Miami.
In 12 games with the Las Vegas Raiders last year, he recorded just 22 carries for yards. He clearly would not be the number one option, but could serve as a rotational player when Wright and Gordon need a break.
Joe Mixon
The Dolphins could look to add Mixon if he clears the medical concerns that cost him the entire 2025 season. If his foot is healthy, and that is obviously a question mark, he could still be the played that picked up 1,016 yards in 2024 with the Houston Texans.
He could be a workhorse, taking a large number of carries, but he is not going to be a direct replacement for Achane. Miami could consider him as the second option, letting Wright lead the group.
Nick Chubb
Chubb just re-signed with the Cleveland Browns to ceremony retire as a member of the team, but the Dolphins could look to sign him for the remainder of the year. Wright would likely remain the top option for Miami, but Chubb could be a more physical rotational playe with him. He might slide ahead of Gordon on the depth chart once he is fully engaged in the offense.
Chubb sustained a knee injury in 2023 and did not return to full form in 2024 or 2025. He only has 224 carries and 838 yards the last two seasons.
Cam Akers
Akers is only 27 years old, so there is potential to still land a running back with potential to reach. However, after being a second-round pick in 2020, he has played for five different teams in seven different stretches. He was at his best with his first team, the Los Angeles Rams, from 2020 through 2023, and he has a great combination of speed and power.
But, in 2025, he only appeared in three games with no carries for Seattle. He would only be a rotational player with the Dolphins, giving Wright a break when needed.
Other options
Other players Miami could consider include Dalvin Cook, Antonio Gibson, D’Onta Foreman, Ronald Jones II, Alexander Mattison, and Miles Sanders. Would you consider any of them? Was there someone not on the list you would consider?
items.titleTR: De’Von Achane injury: What free agents are available for Miami Dolphins?

There is no information indicating that any addition has been selected or that talks are underway.

items.descriptionTR:
Kyler Murray is off to a rough start. Meanwhile, Geno Smith and Kirk Cousins are balling out for the Jets and Raiders, respectively.
It’s never too early to panic in the NFL, and Kyler Murray has given Vikings fans ample reason to be concerned through two starts.
Murray looked awful in 11 snaps before suffering a concussion against the Packers in Week 1, and he was arguably even worse from start to finish in Minnesota’s 23-16 win over Tampa Bay on Sunday.
If you rewind time to February, before the Vikings signed Murray to a one-year contract, they were rumored to be interested in free agent Geno Smith and former Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins.
“I’ve also heard that the Vikings are considering Murray and Smith as they outline their veteran quarterback plan,” ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported on March 1. “Tua Tagovailoa and (Kirk) Cousins are also on their radar. Some I’ve talked to are breaking those four into two tiers, with Murray and Smith in the first group.”
Smith wound up being traded from the Raiders to the Jets just days before the Vikings signed Murray. But it’s not like the Vikings couldn’t have outbid the Jets, who gave up a 2026 sixth-round pick for Smith and a 2026 seventh-round draft pick.
Instead, the Vikings held onto their draft capital and signed Murray to a one-year, $1.3 million deal. Smith’s deal with New York pays him $3.3 million for one season.
Smith has been awesome for the Jets, completing 75.8 percent of his passes for 783 yards, four touchdowns, and no interceptions. Against Detroit on Sunday, Smith completed 31 of 37 passes and threw three touchdowns despite playing without his No. 2 receiver, Adonai Mitchell.

￼
Sep 27, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith (7) throws the ball against the Detroit Lions during the first quarter at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images

Everyone knew that Smith could be a stud in Minnesota’s offense, just like he was when he torched the NFL with the Seahawks from 2022 to 2024, earning two Pro Bowl selections while throwing 71 touchdown passes and completing 68.5 percent of his attempts.
Smith’s 95.5 passer rating during those three years ranked 14th, just behind Baker Mayfield and Justin Herbert. He was third in completion percentage, fourth in passing yards, eighth in passing touchdowns, and in the top three in both fourth-quarter comebacks and game-winning drives.
Here’s what our Will Ragatz wrote about Smith versus Murray back in March.
“Smith is a better scheme fit in Minnesota than someone like Kyler Murray, given his ability to make the intermediate throws over the middle of the field that Kevin O’Connell loves. Smith is also an outstanding deep-ball thrower, which would sync up well with Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. He’s more willing than Murray to stand in the pocket and make throws under pressure instead of bailing out and looking to scramble. The one scheme concern would be that Smith hasn’t operated much from under center, but there’s no reason to think he’s incapable of doing so.“
Cousins didn’t sign with the Raiders until early April. He was never as realistic since he cost more ($20 million this season), but he might’ve looked pretty darn good wearing purple and gold again. The 38-year-old leads the NFL with nine touchdown passes, having led the Raiders to wins over the Dolphins, Chargers, and Saints, the latter two coming on the road.

￼
Sep 27, 2026; New Orleans, Louisiana, USA; Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) reacts after defeating against the New Orleans Saintsat Caesars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Hinton-Imagn Images

Murray, who at one point against Tampa Bay misfired on 11 of 13 passes, has historically been an accurate passer, so there’s a strong chance that he turns things around after an ugly start. On top of that, the Vikings have started 3-0, thus making the QB transition, as rough as it’s been, easier to stomach.
“I mean, it’s only Week 3. That was my first game, really. And again, like I said, (Jefferson) went down. I think we’re going to get better each and every week,” Murray said Sunday. “Obviously, today we didn’t feel like we played our best game.”
Today was Kyler Murray’s 87th regular season start with at least 10 pass attempts.  His 66.5 passer rating in Tampa is the third-lowest in that sample. It shouldn’t be controversial to suggest that he’s going to play better than he did today.
— Will Ragatz (@WillRagatz) September 28, 2026
Better days are likely ahead for Murray, but with how many times the Vikings have butchered the QB decision — drafting Christian Ponder, never giving Kirk Cousins a great offensive line, allegedly passing on Aaron Rodgers, letting Sam Darnold and Daniel Jones get away, and likely whiffing on J.J. McCarthy — it’s hard to not to worry when Murray gets off to a bad start.
We are in the age of big media consolidation and content networks. But even with the proliferation of AI, nothing can beat the quality and inherent knowledge of local sports journalism. Our writing room consists of a Wildcat, a Gopher, and even a Mustang. We know the Minnesota towns and the great names that played on its diamonds, courts, fields or rinks. Murray signed a one-year, $1.3 million contract with the Vikings. items.descriptionTR:
"We're 3-1, I feel like we're 0-4, I can tell you that's how I feel," Kyle Whittingham said about Michigan football's emotional roller coaster start.
It's not just the fans who've felt the up-and-down swings that defined Michigan football's month of September.
In the first four games of the Kyle Whittingham era, three have been decided by one possession while two were decided on the final play of the game with touchdowns that flipped the result as time expired. The first went Michigan's way, when Bryce Underwood found JJ Buchanan on a 47-yard Hail Mary to stave off a Western Michigan upset and survive 13-12 in the season-opener.
In Week 4, it was the opposite. The Wolverines gave up two touchdown drives in the fourth quarter (they hadn't allowed a fourth quarter touchdown all year prior) including an 11-play, 91-yard drive over the final 1:48 of the game that ended with a 16-yard touchdown pass from Hank Brown to Reece Vander Zee to stun U-M with a 20-19 loss.
Two days later, much like the fan base, the team is still licking its wounds. That includes the head coach.
[ MUST LISTEN: Make "Hail Yes!" your go-to Wolverines podcast, available anywhere you listen to podcasts (Apple, Spotify) or watch live on YouTube . ]


"We're 3-1, I feel like we're 0-4, I can tell you that's how I feel," Whittingham said Monday at his weekly press conference. "But we're 3-1 − one play away from 4-0, one play away from 2-2. So, it's been about three of the four games very close, you know, closely contested games.
"It's been an emotional roller coaster in a way."
It's not just the loss, but how it happened. Michigan had multiple chances to put the game away with its four-minute offense, but instead went three-and-out. Offensive coordinator Jason Beck called three consecutive run plays instead of allowing Bryce Underwood even the option to pass (he could've been instructed to simply take a sack or slide to ensure the clock kept running if U-M was worried about saving Iowa time), a conservative approach that ultimately led to Michigan punting just after the two-minute timeout.
Then on defense, U-M had its hands on a potential interception multiple times and dropped each opportunity. After that, Zeke Berry committed a personal foul after Iowa was staring at a fourth-and-12. Whittingham called it "unnecessary."
It led to a tipped pass that picked up 29 yards and gave Iowa one final shot at the end zone with 2 seconds remaining; another play that may not have happened had it not been for John Henry Daley getting injured on the play, staying down and forcing an official timeout.
RELATED: Michigan football finally burned after playing with fire in September
Then, U-M had a questionable defensive play call, going with press-man coverage that forced defensive backs to run with their back to the quarterback. On top of it, one of the linebackers was spying quarterback Hank Brown − a seemingly poor decision because it not only took one man away from coverage, but also was one fewer pass rusher.
"It was such a deflating loss because we had it," Whittingham said. "We snatched defeat from the jaws of victory type, you know the old saying, but again, credit Iowa. I mean, that's nothing new to them. That is their game to a T. Hang around, hang around, hang around. Win at the end.
"That's who they've been for years, and so unfortunately for us it played out pretty much how they script it."
Now, No. 24 Michigan (3-1, 0-1 Big Ten) travels to Minneapolis for its first road game of the season against Minnesota (3-1, 1-0 Big Ten), which comes into the contest feeling pretty good about itself after beating Washington 27-24 on the road, leading by two scores nearly the entire way.
Michigan had the benefit of four consecutive home games to open the season, something Whittingham said he's never had in more than two decades as a head coach, and was one play away from leaving with all types of momentum.
The offense was better, with Bryce Underwood throwing for a career-high 276 yards and two scores. For the first time in four years, two U-M wide receivers had more than 100 yards receiving in a game.
Whittingham said a lot is "trending in the right direction."
Still, there's no doubt Saturday left a mark. But with a new month on the horizon and new challenges ahead, U-M's head coach doesn't believe the Wolverines' hopes for making the College Football Playoff are dashed.
"By no means, I can’t imagine that one loss is going to do that," Whittingham said. "There’s still a ton of football to be played. We’ve got eight more conference games. So in our opinion – I guess there’s a scenario or two where it’s not in our control – but we feel like everything’s going to be within our control still going forward."
Tony Garcia is the Michigan beat writer for the Detroit Free Press. Email him at apgarcia@freepress.com and follow him on X at @RealTonyGarcia.
This article originally appeared on Detroit Free Press: Kyle Whittingham: 'Feel like we're 0-4' after Michigan's emotional start

A story that had it all, from painful defeats to everlasting victories, will come to an end. It will happen on October 6, when Lionel Messi plays his final match with the Argentina national team. When things are going awry, the Albiceleste will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause
It isn’t quite over yet. Lionel Messi will return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.
Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.

Pope Leo XIV on Monday called European leaders to "sacrifice certain positions" on the war in Ukraine for the sake of peace, in what was his strongest political statement yet on Europe.
Speaking in French as he concluded a four-day tour of France, the US-born Pope spoke of the devastating impact and "senseless slaughter" caused by the return of war in Europe since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"We need to commit ourselves to patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiation and to be willing to give up some positions for the greater good of peace," Pope Leo said. "The search of peace in Europe, as throughout the world, must not be confused with a naive form of pacifism."
Standing next to French President Emmanuel Macron, who this summer approved a defence budget increase of €6.5 billion ($7.4 billion) over the next two years, Pope Leo warned against the continent's rearmament. Many European governments, including France, have provided strong financial support for Ukraine's war effort and fear further Russian attacks.
'Stem the tide of war'
"Promoting peace is an active task," Pope Leo said, without mentioning Ukraine. "Today we must ask whether we are truly making creative efforts to advance world peace, or whether we are simply seeking to stem the tide of war and better prepare ourselves for wars that we assume are still to come."
￼
Neither Russia nor Ukraine has shown willingness to concede land after four years of war. Discussions appear at a standstill despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week meeting US President Donald Trump Trump in New York for talks.
Mr Macron, who joined Pope Leo in the north-eastern city of Metz at the last minute for the final Mass of his tour, thanked Pope Leo for his visit, which provided France with a rare moment of unity amid deep political polarisation ahead of a presidential election next year. "You sensed, I hope, a fervent, united and happy nation. I thank you immensely for that," Mr Macron told the head of the Catholic Church.
Pope Leo also tackled the controversial topic of migration in Europe, which this year toughened its rules concerning migrants and asylum seekers. "We must grasp the historical significance of what is taking place, namely an unprecedented encounter between peoples and cultures, which calls us to rediscover our roots in new and creative ways, while at the same time listening carefully to others," he said. "To welcome a person means to integrate them as if they were part of one's own family."
'Lies and deceit'
International and law multilateralism must continue to be championed by Europe, Pope Leo said. "Relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised," he said. "People boast of lies and deceit. Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learnt to cultivate and preserve."
￼
Attending the speeches were a limited number of European leaders despite the French presidency extending an invitation to all EU 27 heads of state. The city of Metz has high significance in European political history as a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation.
Among those present were Prince Albert II of Monaco and his wife Princess Charlene, Luxembourg's Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Grand Duc Guillaume V of Luxembourg and Grand Duchess Stephanie of Luxembourg. Germany was represented by Anke Rehlinger, minister-president of the German state of Saarland.
items.titleTR: Pope Leo urges Europe to 'give up ground' for the sake of peace in Ukraine

He also opposed the idea that rearmament is the solution. The report states that these remarks came in the context of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
