items.descriptionTR: The bureau has not yet publicly confirmed a breach, but has told its agents that their personal information and Social Security numbers were exposed.
items.titleTR: FBI reportedly declares ‘cyber security incident’ after hackers steal agents’ personal data

slots.packetSpot:
Following a cyberattack reported to have targeted the FBI’s job application portal, the agency’s agents and support staff are reportedly being notified that their personal information was stolen. Names, addresses, job titles and Social Security numbers are said to have been exposed; records relating to blood and urine samples, as well as psychiatric reports, are also alleged to be among some of the stolen data.

The FBI had previously said it was aware of a group’s claim of a cyberattack, but that data theft had not yet been identified. The agency was later reported to have described the incident as a “cybersecurity incident” in an internal notification to employees. A group called ShinyHunters claimed to possess extensive data relating to the FBI and applicants, and also alleged that access had been gained through a vulnerability in an Oracle PeopleSoft server.

The FBI’s job portal is reported to remain offline. While it remains unclear whether Congress has been notified, a national security expert described the incident as a “counterintelligence disaster” for the US government, drawing attention to risks such as profiling, phishing and approaches by foreign intelligence services.
slots.packetTitle: A reported breach at the FBI

items.descriptionTR: On Equity, we discussed how Meta's AI announcement managed to steal the spotlight from OpenAI and Anthropic.
items.titleTR: Can Muse overcome Meta’s trust issues?

items.descriptionTR: Meta's Muse AI personal agent will work over your credit card spending if you don't mind the invasion. How big a threat is it to the subscription economy?
items.titleTR: Meta's Muse agent is attacking one of the economy's most profitable weak spots

slots.packetSpot:
Meta’s Muse stands out as an AI assistant extending into personal spending. Functions such as finding and cancelling recurring subscriptions, detecting duplicate charges and searching for unclaimed money open up space for more direct intervention in consumers’ financial decisions.

One person who tried Muse said the assistant helped them find unclaimed money and that they were expecting a cheque in the mail; however, they viewed this as a one-off demonstration rather than a reason for sustained use. The prospect of access to sensitive data such as credit card and email information raises questions about trust in Meta, privacy and the company’s advertising-based business model.

It is said that tools that make subscription cancellations easier could put pressure on companies that benefit from consumers’ forgetfulness and the difficulty of cancellation processes. It is suggested that if assistants like Muse direct household cash into higher-yielding accounts, they could also affect banks’ cheap deposits. Amazon, meanwhile, blocked Muse from shopping on its site, saying its access violated its terms of use.

At a time when OpenAI and Anthropic are focusing more on enterprise use, Meta is trying to embed AI in everyday consumer life. This direction makes it harder to separate the promise of usefulness from the question of control over personal data.
slots.packetTitle: Muse moves into the spending stream

items.descriptionTR: Analysts warn an export ban could backfire, pushing up global diesel prices and potentially triggering higher U.S. gasoline prices as refiners adjust.
items.titleTR: Trump ‘very seriously’ considering diesel export ban as global supply crunch worsens

slots.packetSpot:
Under political pressure from rising fuel prices and ahead of the November midterm elections, Donald Trump said they were considering a ban on diesel exports “very seriously.” He had previously said that a decision would be made soon, “one way or the other.” However, no measure has yet been put into effect; Energy Secretary Chris Wright said restrictions rather than an outright ban were being considered. According to Politico, the administration was preparing a plan for a 90-day ban.

The price of a gallon of diesel in the United States was about $6.50 on Friday, according to AAA data; that level is just below the record. The report says that clashes between the United States and Iran, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, reduced flows from Russia and the Middle East, attacks on Russian refineries and the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz have contributed to a global supply squeeze.

Limiting exports by the United States, the world’s largest diesel exporter, could probably initially lower domestic diesel prices, according to Morgan Stanley strategists; however, the same strategists warned that it could raise global diesel prices and feed back into U.S. gasoline prices through changes in refinery operations. Benedict George of Argus Media said the United States had supplied about half of Europe’s diesel imports in recent months; any restriction could push prices in Europe and premiums over crude oil to unprecedented levels. The American Petroleum Institute also argued that export restrictions could worsen refining problems and harm consumers.
slots.packetTitle: Diesel's exit door

items.descriptionTR: England will begin the next phase of their preparations for the 50-over World Cup without Jos Buttler after the former captain was ruled out of their upcoming white-ball tour of Pakistan.
items.titleTR: Buttler ruled out of Pakistan white-ball tour

slots.packetSpot:
Jos Buttler will not take part in England’s white-ball tour of Pakistan after suffering a hamstring injury in the second ODI against Sri Lanka. McCullum confirmed that Buttler will not be in Pakistan; in his absence, with the player also set to miss next month’s 50-over tri-series, England will continue their preparations for the 50-over World Cup by giving wicketkeeper-batter Jordan Cox a broader opportunity.

Buttler initially left the field because of the injury during the match at Headingley, before returning to the field. There is still no assurance over whether Buttler, who missed the series-deciding match at the Kia Oval, will be fit for the Australia tour in November. McCullum said it was difficult to predict the timeframe for his return.

items.descriptionTR: Bruno Fernandes, Cody Gakpo and Patrick Dorgu all join the international break's high-profile injury list after suffering issues that have curtailed their involvement in Nations League matches.

The first international break of the 2026-27 men's football season has stretched to three weeks with the traditional October break removed; teams are playing four international matches instead of two during this period. Alongside Bruno Fernandes, Cody Gakpo and Patrick Dorgu, Alexander Isak, Kai Havertz, Brian Brobbey, Dan Ballard, Kylian Mbappe and Jamal Musiala have also come into focus because of injury or withdrawal.

Gakpo left the game in the 17th minute of the Netherlands' 2-1 win over Serbia in Belgrade, holding the lower part of his right leg. Liverpool confirmed that the player had left the Netherlands squad and returned to the club. Netherlands head coach Xavi said the problem was in his ankle, but that its severity was not yet known.

According to Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus, Fernandes played against Wales despite carrying an injury from Manchester United. Fernandes was not included in the squad for the Norway match. Dorgu, meanwhile, left the pitch after 30 minutes in Denmark's 2-0 win over Wales and is expected to return to Manchester for further tests on a suspected hamstring problem.

Brandon McNulty reportedly won the men's elite road race in Montreal. The result brought the United States its first men's elite road race world championship since Lance Armstrong's victory in Oslo in 1993.

Kevin Pietersen has begun a specialist mentoring role with England’s white-ball team, which will run until the 50-over World Cup in 2027. Speaking to Sky Sports Cricket, Pietersen said head coach Brendon McCullum had asked him to challenge him; he said he would question the areas that would develop the players.

slots.packetSpot:
Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha says his life has not been the same since his breakthrough at the 2026 World Cup. Vozinha, who was reported to have made seven saves in the goalless opening match against Spain, saw his Instagram follower count rise from around 56,000 before the match to more than 1 million by its end; within a few days, it had reached around 14 million.

Vozinha said the attention had reduced his peace and privacy; outside, he encountered requests for photos and autographs, as well as people filming him. He stated that if he had to choose between his life today and his previous life, he would prefer the latter. items.descriptionTR: BERLIN, Sept 28 - Germany on Monday vowed continued support for the International Criminal Court, ahead of a trip by its foreign minister to the Hague-based court that is currently in the US administration's crosshairs.
items.titleTR: Germany vows support for ICC as Trump escalates pressure on court

slots.packetSpot:
Germany pledged strong support for the court at a time when the United States is reported to be increasing pressure on the International Criminal Court. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany would help ensure that the ICC can continue operating even under pressure.

Wadephul described support for the ICC as part of Germany’s historical responsibility. He was scheduled to visit the court in The Hague and meet his Dutch counterpart, Tom Berendsen.

The United States does not recognise the ICC; it is reported to be increasing its sanctions against the court and its representatives. Donald Trump also called on ICC member states to withdraw from the court at the UN General Assembly last week. Since 2002, the ICC has prosecuted the gravest crimes, including genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
slots.packetTitle: Berlin stands with The Hague

items.descriptionTR: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".
items.titleTR: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class

items.descriptionTR: ROME, Sept 28 - New rules to limit the number of foreign pupils in Italian classrooms, introduced by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, are set to affect at most just a few hundred children nationwide, according to experts and a Reuters analysis of public data.
items.titleTR: Italy decree limiting foreign pupils in classrooms could have near-zero impact

slots.packetSpot:
The Giorgia Meloni government's school package combines a ban on face coverings including the burqa and niqab with a 30 percent cap for students with limited Italian proficiency. The government presents the measure as a step that will support integration and prevent “ghetto classes”; Giuseppe Valditara says the limit concerns language, not citizenship.

The ban does not cover the hijab. The decree can take effect immediately, but must receive parliamentary approval within 60 days. Exceptions are envisaged for students born in Italy or who have spent a certain period in the Italian school system; it is stated that additional Italian-language instruction may be provided where necessary.

According to expert Costanzo Ranci and Reuters’ review based on public data, the student cap could affect around 300 children nationwide; the number may not exceed 1,000, or could even remain at zero. The government did not disclose its own impact estimate. While the opposition describes the measure as propaganda, Roberto Vannacci supports the measures.
slots.packetTitle: Meloni’s line in the classroom

items.descriptionTR: [Shabelle] Baidoa, Somalia -- A combat broke out in Baidoa between forces supporting South West State leader Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe and fighters loyal to former South West President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen.
items.titleTR: Somalia: Fresh Battle Renewed in Somalia's Baidoa Town

slots.packetSpot:
Renewed fighting is reportedly under way in Baidoa between forces supporting Madobe and fighters loyal to Laftagareen. While the political dispute over the administration and future leadership of South West State continues, the Somali federal government and the Madobe administration have not officially confirmed the new fighting in the city.

Pro-Laftagareen forces are reported to be approaching the outskirts of the city, while an earlier claim that parts of Baidoa had been seized has not been independently verified. There is also no verification of claims regarding military movements within the city, control of buildings and the use of drones.

The South West Peace, Unity and Development Council reportedly called for a ceasefire and negotiations after holding talks with the two sides. City residents are concerned that possible new clashes could disrupt security, daily life and essential services.

items.descriptionTR:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm
In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.
As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
items.titleTR: Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen

items.descriptionTR: Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
items.titleTR: Inside Djibouti refugee camp for thousands fleeing Houthi advance in Yemen

items.descriptionTR: 809 new casualties recorded between Sept. 19-26, bringing total since Aug. 6 to 4,481, including 838 deaths
items.titleTR: Yemen casualties rising by around 100 per day amid escalating conflict: WHO

slots.packetSpot:
The effects of renewed fighting in Yemen on civilian life are becoming visible in different ways. As the fighting drew closer in Taiz's al-Waziyah district, Muneer Farie and his family went to a camp for displaced people in al-Shimayateyn; Muneer and his brother began selling socks and cheap goods around the camp's markets instead of going to school. Musaab Ibn Umayr School in Taiz also closed after a missile that landed nearby caused panic among students; more than 600 students at the school were deprived of education.

More than 130,000 people are reported to have been displaced in the latest fighting in Yemen. Following clashes on the western coast, thousands also crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by boat and reached a refugee camp in Djibouti. According to the World Health Organization, 809 new cases were recorded between 19 and 26 September, including 645 injured and 164 dead; since 6 August, the total has risen to 4,481, including 838 deaths. The organization says the heaviest burden of casualties has been seen in Lahij.
slots.packetTitle: The civilian cost of war in Yemen

items.titleTR: The killing of women is not a series of unconnected tragedies in South Africa

With South Africa facing soaring femicide rates, the ongoing UN General Assembly in New York highlights the urgent need to address the global crisis and backlash against women's rights.
items.titleTR: Global war on women through SA's eyes

items.descriptionTR: The Ekurhuleni killings have intensified fears over South Africa’s femicide crisis, exposing women’s daily vulnerability and persistent failures in policing, prevention and accountability.
items.titleTR: EAST RAND KILLING FIELDS: ‘Men who kill, kill with impunity’— Ekurhuleni murders expose SA’s femicide failures

items.descriptionTR: Many South African men insist they’re ‘fine’ while seven women in the country are killed daily. But personal exceptions cannot erase the evidence: femicide demands an honest audit of masculinity, complicity — and silence, too.
items.titleTR: Ledgers of femicide: Why SA men think they’re the exception

slots.packetSpot:
Femicide and gender-based violence have been declared a national disaster in South Africa. Nine women have been killed in Ekurhuleni since July, while the discovery of a woman's body in Soweto has heightened concerns; police have not confirmed the existence of a serial killer.

According to published research, the country's intimate partner femicide rate is among the highest in the world. Data from one study for 2020–21 state that fewer than one-fifth of femicide cases resulted in convictions, while police were unable to identify a perpetrator in 44.5 percent of cases. In the same discussion, threats, controlling behaviour, misogynistic attitudes and perceptions of impunity emerge as parts of a continuum that can extend to lethal violence.

Lawrence Chamurwa Mudzinganyama allegedly threatened three women at a restaurant in Sandton after they rejected his advances. It was reported that he was taken into custody after footage of the incident circulated on 20 September and is expected to appear in court on 1 October 2026; the legal process has not yet concluded.

The 81st UN General Assembly in New York also forms part of the backdrop to discussions on women's rights, equality and security. According to UN Women's 2026 gender outlook, 171 years are needed to close the inequality gap; within this framework, it is argued that local mechanisms for protection, prevention and accountability cannot be considered separately from international rights debates.
slots.packetTitle: The continuum of femicide

items.descriptionTR:
Photographer Alexandre Bagdassarian spent eight months following the daily lives of children in a prison system criticised for the long time spent in cells
The cells of the children were difficult places for me to photograph because they are impersonal and intimate at the same time. Once inside, you quickly find yourself going in circles, with nowhere to go. Your gaze settles on the very few elements that make up the space: a window, cell bars, a rudimentary bed, a plank serving as a desk, and sometimes a book or a few drawings.
Sometimes, due to staff shortages, a young person may spend as much as 23 hours a day in their cell. This and the low levels of access to educational and sports activities have been criticised by Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture.
The cell windows directly overlook the prison yard, a mandatory one-hour stop each day
items.titleTR: ‘I sleep with all my clothes on to protect my privacy’: a glimpse into life inside a child prison in France

items.descriptionTR: The BBC goes inside the prison where prisoners were trapped in stifling, cramped conditions.
items.titleTR: 'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria

slots.packetSpot:
Accounts of child detention conditions in France show that, because of staff shortages, some children can remain in their cells for up to 23 hours a day; access to education and sports activities is also limited. While the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture has criticised these conditions, detained children describe the loss of privacy, disciplinary cells and the psychological distress caused by confinement.

In Minna, Nigeria, it was reported that 33 people in custody died in a small cell, while four others later died in hospital. Survivors’ accounts of extreme heat, humidity, lack of water and inadequate ventilation are at the centre of the investigation; authorities initially pointed to diphtheria. The causes of death and responsibility have not yet been determined; it was announced that 24 personnel from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps are in custody.
slots.packetTitle: The dangerous face of confinement

items.descriptionTR:
Colombian Julián Palacios contracted a bacterial infection during his detention of more than 600 days. Now, free, he seeks medical care ￼
Colombian Julián Palacios Obregón spent 650 days in immigration detention in the United States. He was sick for most of that time. A month after being transferred to the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington state, he began vomiting and suffering diarrhea with fecal incontinence that forced him to wear diapers. Although he was prescribed antibiotics that temporarily improved symptoms caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, the underlying problem repeatedly returned: he remained exposed to cloudy water and to food he often described as raw or foul-smelling.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: ‘An incomplete happiness’: An activist wins his freedom after nearly two years of medical neglect at an ICE facility

items.descriptionTR:
Aminata Seck’s detention shows the bargain facing international college athletes: universities eagerly recruit them, but support can disappear when their immigration status becomes precarious
Earlier this week, news broke for the first time that Senegalese Division II Kentucky State women’s basketball player Aminata Seck was abducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport on 7 August during a trip to attend the HBCU All-Star game in New York. Seck is listed as a Kentucky State senior and last year started 20 of 26 games, earning third-team all-conference honors and an SIAC Elite 16 award for academic achievement. According to a lawyer involved with her case, Sadiqa Reynolds, Seck has been moved through four different ICE facilities since her initial apprehension: Clay County, Chicago, Clark County and Grayson County. Reynolds noted that the reason for Seck’s imprisonment was a missed student visa deadline – what she characterized as “a paperwork situation” – due to back surgery. Reynolds also said that Seck has been suffering from an ACL injury while detained and has received only ibuprofen but no proper medical care.
ICE arrests in Kentucky have risen by 70% this year.
Nathan Kalman-Lamb is Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of New Brunswick and co-host of The End of Sport podcast.
Simran Kaur Sethi is Assistant Professor of Sport Leadership at the University of Kentucky where she studies equity and inclusion for international college athletes.
Derek Silva is Professor of Sociology and Criminology at King’s University College at Western University and co-host of The End of Sport podcast.
items.titleTR: ICE has abducted a college athlete. What are the NCAA and universities going to do about it?

slots.packetSpot:
The cases of Colombian activist Julián Palacios Obregón and Senegalese university basketball player Aminata Seck, held in U.S. immigration detention, highlight reported disruptions in access to healthcare.

Palacios Obregón said that during his time at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, he experienced recurring gastrointestinal ailments, delayed appointments and an inadequate response to his acute pain. The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington ordered his release on September 11, 2026, ruling that the repeated failure to provide adequate treatment, including a recommended colonoscopy, had turned detention into something punitive in nature and in violation of his right to due process. The Department of Homeland Security, however, denied the claim that he had not received appropriate medical care.

Seck’s lawyers reported that the athlete, who was taken into ICE detention after missing a deadline related to her student visa, was initially given only ibuprofen for an anterior cruciate ligament injury in her knee, suffered seizures and did not receive adequate care. Deadly risks persist for those who expose environmental destruction, corruption or rights violations. Global Witness’s report says it was able to verify the killings of 124 land and environmental defenders worldwide in 2025; 12 of them took place in the Philippines. According to the report, 85 percent of the cases occurred in Latin America and 12 percent in Asia; one person each was also killed in India, Indonesia and Turkey.

The report describes the Philippines as Asia’s deadliest country for environmental defenders for the 13th consecutive year. items.descriptionTR:
In Nate Silver’s aggregate of national polls, Donald Trump’s net approval has dropped to a new record low of -23.
In his forecast model, Democrats are the clear favourites to gain control of the US federal Senate at November 3 midterm elections, and overwhelming favourites to gain control of the House of Representatives.
If disruption caused by the Iran war continues until the midterm elections, with increased petrol prices and inflation, Republicans are likely to lose control of both the House and the Senate, perhaps with huge losses.
However, if the disruption eases again and petrol prices fall back before the midterms, I believe Republicans will do better than they are now and may retain control of the Senate.
I can say this because Trump’s net approval and the generic ballot were better for Republicans in early September, soon after a low in petrol prices.
Trump’s ratings
In analyst Nate Silver’s aggregate of US national polls, Trump’s net approval is at a new record low -23.0. Currently, 60.4% disapprove of his performance and 37.4% approve.
Trump’s net approval was -19.7 in my September 14 article. It had improved to -18.7 on September 4 before falling back.
Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term, with Trump’s first term the closest at -11.6.
On four issues tracked by Silver, Trump’s net approval is -13.0 on immigration, -28.3 on trade, -32.1 on the economy and -46.4 on inflation. Since my September 14 article, Trump’s net approval on immigration, trade and the economy have all dropped one to two points.
Silver also has an aggregate of US support for the Iran war. Currently, 57.9% are opposed to the Iran war while 33.5% support it, for a net support of -24.4, down from -20.1 in my September 14 article.
Midterm elections on November 3
All 435 federal House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 senators will be up for election at November 3 midterm elections.
In 2024 elections, Republicans won the House by 220–215 over Democrats and the Senate by 53–47. Owing to Vice President JD Vance’s potential tie-breaking vote, Democrats need at least a four-seat gain to win Senate control.
I previously wrote that, owing to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats need at least a four-point margin in the generic ballot to have a good chance to win the House majority. The Senate is more skewed to Republicans as every state has two senators. Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win the Senate on a uniform swing.
In Silver’s midterm election forecast model, the generic ballot gives Democrats a 51.4–42.3 lead over Republicans, a 9.1-point margin (8.2 points in my September 14 article). Democrats’ lead had dropped to 7.4 points on September 4.
Polls that screen for likely voters usually give Democrats larger leads than polls that ask registered voters. Democrats are more likely to vote at lower turnout elections like the midterms than Republicans, when Trump is not on the ballot.
Silver’s model gives Democrats a 69% chance to win the Senate and a 91% chance to win the House, respectively 57% and 86% on September 14. Democratic chances to win the Senate had fallen to a low of 50% on September 7, and their chances of winning the House had dropped to 81% on September 3.
While uniform swing indicates that Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win control of the Senate, Silver’s model has Democrats as the favourites to win with a 6–7 point margin in the generic ballot. In the House, Democrats are favourites if they win by 3–4 points.
Democrats now lead by two to five points in Senate contests in Texas, Ohio, Alaska and Iowa. Trump won all these states by double-digit margins in 2024. This explains why Democrats are the favourites to gain control of the Senate. Furthermore, Republicans are trailing an independent in Nebraska by 0.2 points and only leading a Democrat in Kansas by 1.3 points.
A bad spot for Democrats is Maine, which should be the easiest Senate gain for them as Kamala Harris defeated Trump in Maine by 6.9 points. But Republican incumbent Susan Collins has led Democrat Troy Jackson in the last two Maine Senate polls, including a three-point lead in a Siena poll for The New York Times.
The two key items that could go wrong for Democrats are a markedly improved economy by November for most Americans – not just the stock market – and a systematic error in which Republicans overperform the polls.
Economic data
Americans are currently paying an average of US$4.48 (A$6.69) a gallon for regular petrol (gasoline in the US). Owing to profits and taxes, the retail price of petrol will be higher than the commodity price.
The commodity price of petrol has surged from a low of US$2.99 (A$4.27) a gallon on August 27 to US$3.49 (A$4.89) now, but down from US$3.52 (A$5.02) on Wednesday. The Iran war high was US$3.76 (A$5.36) on May 18. Before the Iran war began, it was under US$2.
In Silver’s models, Trump and Republicans were at a high in early September, shortly after the August 27 low point in petrol prices.
There appears to be a lag time from changes in the oil price being passed on to petrol. The international benchmark Brent oil peaked at US$108.75 (A$155.17) a barrel on September 15, but fell to US$99.25 (A$141.61) on Tuesday before rising to its current US$105.81 (A$150.97). This implies there should be at least a short-lived drop in petrol prices soon.
After large gains in the three sessions from September 17–21, the benchmark US S&P stock market index is down just 1.2% from its August 13 peak, but up 10.9% from its peak in the week before the Iran war began in late February. It’s up 16.9% from its worst point in the Iran war in late March.
While the AI boom is assisting the stock market, Silver said a poll for Politico had 63% thinking there was at least a moderate risk of AI destroying humanity, compared with 22% who thought there was no or a very small risk. The splits between Trump and Harris 2024 voters were not wide, with Trump voters favouring at least a moderate risk by 61–29 and Harris voters by 70–21.
￼
Adrian Beaumont does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term.

As the November 3 midterm elections approach, polls and forecasting models show Democrats in an advantageous position for the House of Representatives, while a more competitive but possible path is emerging for the Senate. Decision Desk HQ puts the probability of Democrats taking the House at 72 percent and the Senate at 54 percent. Nate Silver’s model puts those figures at 91 percent and 69 percent, respectively.

Charlie Cook has long seen Democrats retaking the House as nearly certain; he now also considers a change of hands in the Senate “very realistic.” By contrast, general ballot preference polls do not directly measure the outcome of individual races. Republicans’ financial advantage, candidates’ local strength, districting arrangements, turnout and possible polling errors could alter the picture.

Trump’s approval rating ranges between 32 percent and 37 percent across different measures; in Silver’s national polling average, his net approval is minus 23. The economy, inflation, immigration, tariffs, fuel prices and the Iran war are being associated with voter dissatisfaction. Some Republican candidates’ openly distancing themselves from Trump is also seen as one sign of this pressure.

Texas, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Michigan, Maine, Nebraska and Kansas stand out in Senate races. Although Democrats’ advantage in some states has changed the probability calculation for the Senate, an improvement in economic and energy conditions, along with Republicans outperforming the polls, could restore the balance.

items.descriptionTR:
A few tentative displays of independence among Republicans have expanded in recent days into a stampede, as candidates furiously distance themselves from President Trump ahead of the midterm elections. “This is shaping up to be a nightmare political environment for every Republican, everywhere—period, full stop,” one Texas-based political consultant told us, speaking anonymously to provide a frank assessment. Noting that gas prices across the country are on average $4.50 a gallon, the consultant described the atmosphere as “a fucking disaster for anyone in a competitive race.”
The contrast with the midterm elections of Trump’s first term is particularly stark. An October 2018 rally in Richmond, Kentucky, was a political show of force by a president whose hold on the Republican Party was as firm as bedrock. The opening speaker, Republican State Senator Ralph Alvarado, hailed Trump’s many accomplishments as “amazing to see.” Senator Rand Paul crowed that Trump “exceeds my expectations” almost every day. Representative Andy Barr, whom Trump had come to town to endorse, praised the president as “a man of action” who “gets results,” prompting the thousands of MAGA faithful in attendance to erupt in cheers.
Kentucky Republicans have been fawning over Trump for the past decade. But now, as the war with Iran drags on and Trump’s approval ratings crater, even they are starting to keep the president at a distance. Barr, who is running for an open Senate seat, and Alvarado, who is running to replace him in the House, have each recently scrubbed mentions of Trump’s name from prominent portions of their campaign websites. Paul has been more vocal, repeatedly clashing with the White House over the Iran war and the ballooning national debt.
The notably lukewarm embrace of Trump from Republican candidates in Kentucky, a state that he won by more than 30 points in 2024, is just one indicator of the president’s loosening grip on a party he has dominated for the past decade.
Republican candidates seeking a reason to distance themselves from an unpopular president have a buffet of options to choose from. The war in Iran, which began almost seven months ago, has sent diesel prices to record highs. The United States is in an escalating trade war with Canada. The national debt, the elimination of which was once an obsession of conservatives, has ballooned to more than $40 trillion—and that’s before the $5,000 government checks Trump has promised to dole out if Republicans win. Inflation and interest rates, which Trump pledged to bring down, remain elevated. Gas and food are more expensive than they were a year ago, and mortgage rates passed 7 percent yesterday.
The president’s approval ratings on these and other issues are abysmal. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday found that his approval rating has dipped to 32 percent—the lowest that pollster has measured at any point in his political career. Only 17 percent of respondents said they approved of the president’s handling of the cost of living. Barring a major change in the Iran war or the price of diesel, his numbers aren’t likely to change substantially, the Texas-based Republican consultant said. Members of his party were hoping the dynamic would improve, but it hasn’t—giving them little choice but to scramble over one another for the emergency exits.
The list of Republican candidates publicly noting their differences with Trump keeps growing. Many are in states where polls show tighter-than-expected races for the GOP. Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas spoke out this month about Trump’s calls to ban the sale of jets from the Canadian company Bombardier, whose U.S. headquarters are in Wichita. The Senate candidates Mike Rogers in Michigan, Ashley Hinson in Iowa, and Jon Husted in Ohio have each called for a swift end to the war in Iran, noting its impact on gas prices even as Trump has claimed that such hikes are “a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done” there.
Even in Trump’s adopted state of Florida, which he’s won three times, candidates are bailing. Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor, recently updated his campaign website to remove multiple references to Trump—including a photo with the president and a banner noting that he was “TRUMP-ENDORSED,” the Miami Herald reported Tuesday. Last week, Representative María Elvira Salazar released a political ad filmed in front of the White House warning the president that Hispanic voters “feel betrayed” by immigration and deportation policies that have “gone too far.” Marshall, the Kansas senator who has been a vocal supporter of Trump’s immigration crackdowns, shifted his tone this week, asserting that ICE agents conducting raids in his state needed to “coordinate with our local law enforcement.”
Even red-state Republicans who are not on the ballot are seeking daylight between themselves and the president. Senator John Curtis of Utah this week called for an investigation into Trump’s son Don Jr. over corruption allegations, including concerns about a luxurious, days-long party for his wedding that was funded by a Russian oligarch. Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi on Wednesday took to the Senate floor to admonish the White House for giving “brutal” Chinese President Xi Jinping a “lavish welcome” to the U.S. this week.
[Read: The deferential president]
“The midterms are going to be a fucking bloodbath, and we all know it and we all know why,” Representative Nancy Mace, a retiring South Carolina Republican, told us of the president she once enthusiastically supported. She broke with him earlier this year and last week voted to end the Iran war. “We haven’t done what we said we were going to do, and Republicans are the least motivated group to turn out this cycle.”
Trump is not the first president to see members of his party running in the opposite direction in an attempt to salvage their political fortunes. Barack Obama and George W. Bush each steered clear of certain vulnerable members’ districts ahead of challenging midterm elections. Joe Biden, who faced sinking approval ratings during the 2022 midterms, regularly said he would happily campaign with or against any Democrat, if doing so would help them get elected.
But only Trump has demanded extreme loyalty. Stepping out of line was a rarity during the first year and a half of Trump’s second term, which began with a flurry of executive actions that left much of Washington shell-shocked. But Trump could demand fealty for only so long, Russell Riley, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia’s Miller Center, told us. “The cascading opposition to the president on multiple fronts now is important not just because of what it might represent for the midterm election, but more so because it reestablishes a kind of fixed point of orientation in the political universe again, making it possible for those who were persistently disoriented to regain their balance,” he said.
Even as the evidence has mounted that Trump is dragging down his party, the president has highlighted the very positions that have made him unpopular. After it was already clear that public concern over data centers was endangering the campaigns of vulnerable Republicans such as Husted, Trump insulted communities that rejected the projects as places that wanted to end up “backwards and poor.” He has dismissed bipartisan efforts to rein in the dangers of AI, saying he wants technology companies to have freedom to develop what he has begun referring to as “super intelligence.” He has continued to defend the war in Iran—suggesting this week at the United Nations that he might annihilate the entire country—and minimized the economic cost Americans are shouldering as a result.
Trump has also repeatedly told voters to pretend that he was on the ballot. Democrats have been happy to oblige, mentioning the president in 66,000 airings of general-election ads since August 1, according to the political-ad tracking firm AdImpact. (Republicans have mentioned Trump in a mere 7,000 airings.) The president does still have sway over his most die-hard supporters, and the White House provided us with a lengthy list of Republicans who continue to campaign with the president and praise him on social media and in speeches. He is also still deploying the enormous resources of political action committees he controls to help the GOP.
“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” the White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told us in a statement. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
The campaigns of Salazar, Donalds, Alvarado, Barr, Rogers, and Hinson did not respond to our requests for comment. (Salazar has said that she met with Trump after her ad went up and had a cordial conversation about immigration.)
Dozens of Republicans broke with Trump after the January 6 insurrection, only for many to return to the fold after he won office a second time. But for those who have been eager to see the party move on from Trump, the events of the past few weeks mark a potentially more durable shift. Mike Madrid, a Republican strategist and co-founder of the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, told us he has been watching the MAGA movement for a decade, asking: “When is this fever swamp gonna finally break?” He thinks the moment is now. Candidates have begun making the calculation that Trump is more of a liability than an asset, and are de-emphasizing their relationship with him. “This is the first time I’ve ever seen that,” he said.
The fact that it’s happening even in places like Kentucky is telling. In May, Trump successfully intervened in a House primary in the state to punish Thomas Massie for breaking ranks. But things are now very different. Barr, who is widely expected to win the Senate race in November, removed a photo of himself with Trump from the front page of his website and changed the phrase “America First” to “Kentucky First.” (The website still features language describing Barr as the first member of the state’s congressional delegation to endorse Trump.) The campaign website for Alvarado, who is running in the state’s most competitive congressional district, also scrubbed a photo with Trump and replaced multiple references to the president’s name.
When asked about candidates such as Hinson and Rogers publicly calling for an end to the war in Iran, a Republican operative told us that they were “not running away from Trump in his entirety” but instead making specific distinctions while still embracing the president’s broader record. Trump has not lashed out against candidates who are moving away from him. That’s a shift from years past, and his decision to hold his fire may be giving more candidates confidence to pull away. “It’s more that they’re allowed to have disagreements on certain issues with Trump,” the operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said.
Trump has also distanced himself from some Republicans, at least the ones not polling very well. Last month, he told Punchbowl News that voters were “not angry at me, but they are angry at Republicans.” He has repeatedly noted that GOP turnout tends to drop when he is not on the ballot, saying that he viewed such political trends as a kind of personal compliment despite their detrimental consequences for members of his party.
[Read: An electoral mess in Missouri]
The day after the 2018 midterms, when Republicans lost 40 seats in the House, Trump held a press conference and singled out the losing Republican candidates who had rejected his “embrace” during the campaign. “You had some that decided to ‘Let’s stay away, let’s stay away.’ They did very poorly,” he told reporters. “I’m not sure that I should be happy or sad, but I feel just fine about it.” He then went on to mockingly name a handful of the defeated candidates.
It is easy to imagine the president holding a similar news conference this fall, calling out the Republicans who kept him away during the campaign. This time, the list would be much longer.
A president who demanded loyalty is no longer getting it.

The Supreme Court lifted restrictions on the Trump administration's use of the federal SAVE database to help states verify voters' citizenship. The decision also preserves rules limiting large-scale purges of voter rolls close to an election. Three liberal-leaning justices dissented; critics argue that the database could pose problems in terms of reliability and privacy, and that US citizens risk being mistakenly removed from the rolls. The system is reportedly used by 27 states.

The timing and conditions for early and mail-in voting vary by state and, in some places, by local administration. In some states, voters may cast an early ballot without giving a reason, while Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire require specific conditions for this. Some rules concerning deadlines for the delivery of mail ballots could also change depending on a case before the Supreme Court.

In Missouri, meanwhile, the Supreme Court blocked the use in the November election of a 7-1 congressional map said to favor Republicans and ruled that the state must return to its previous 6-2 map. The court said that a new change could disrupt the election while ballots had begun to be mailed. Governor Mike Kehoe expressed disappointment with the decision and said the state would comply with it. Broader redistricting efforts associated with Donald Trump and national Republicans are also continuing in various states.

There are also warnings that independent journalism in the United States faces economic, technological, legal and political pressure; lawsuits and intimidation attempts associated with the Trump administration are said to be worsening this picture. It is argued that the weakening of press freedom could erode constitutional safeguards shaped by Supreme Court rulings, as well as democracy in the United States and around the world.

The debate over Russia-linked hybrid pressure in Europe stretches from verified online disinformation campaigns to suspected sabotage still under investigation, from airspace violations to warnings of possible new operations. The common picture is less one of a single attack being confirmed than of uncertainty becoming part of security policy and everyday life.

The possibility raised for the Mediterranean is also at the centre of this uncertainty. According to CIA information reported by El Mundo, Russia may be planning to send drones to Spain, Italy or France from vessels posing as commercial ships. Macron said France had not been informed by the CIA about this. While experts assess that such a move is possible, they also note that the threat itself may be a psychological tool intended to generate fear and suspicion.

The government in Poland assessed a fire at a Starlink ground station as sabotage; however, the investigation is ongoing and Tusk stressed that there is no certainty. Drone incidents in Moldova and Romania, along with a Russian helicopter that briefly entered Polish airspace, also raised the level of alarm along the border. Sirens, evacuations and preparations for sheltering in Dorohusk show the anxiety created in local life by warnings of a possible attack.

Denmark's assessment describes a limited Russian attack against NATO countries as a very low-probability but increasingly risky possibility. Meanwhile, Russia-linked campaigns conducted through AI-generated fake videos, cloned voices and fabricated news websites have been documented. What the real impact of these efforts is remains unclear; online disinformation is also a method used by other states.

items.descriptionTR:
Ads appearing all over the Internet are trying to scam people.
Researchers say they recently found Google ads delivering a sophisticated tech support scam that freezes the screens of both Windows and Mac devices and displays messages urgently instructing them to phone a bogus call center.
The ads were displayed all over the web, including on high-traffic maps, weather, real-estate, document-hosting, and sports sites. Users who called the number were then urged to pay hefty fees, grant remote access to their devices, or divulge personal information. From August 31 to September 14, security firm Netskope observed users from 619 customer organizations click on the malicious ads, although none of them were actually scammed because Netskope blocked the content.
Roughly 62 percent of the organizations were based in the US, with Japan and Australia accounting for the Nos. 2 and 3 spots. Since the firm has visibility into only a tiny sliver of Internet activity, the number of people exposed to the ads—including those who fell victim to it—is likely much higher. Netskope tracked more than 250 Google Ads campaign IDs across at least 284 legitimate publisher sites.

items.descriptionTR:
Global Village has warned residents not to buy VIP packs for the coming season from unauthorised websites or individual sellers.
The warning comes as the cultural destination in Dubai prepares to open its gates on October 14 for the coming season, which runs until May. Last week, operators opened bookings for the VIP packs, which was followed by a scam warning from Dubai Police, who cautioned the public to watch out for fake websites and social media accounts promoting fraudulent packages.
The popular tourist park emphasised that the exclusive VIP packs are available for purchase only from the official Coca-Cola Arena website (coca-cola-arena.com), urging that “no other website, seller or individual is authorised to sell these packs”.
In a statement, Global Village stressed that purchasing from unauthorised sources could leave the buyer open to fraud and that packs acquired in this way may be cancelled or deactivated under the terms and conditions.
Scammers imitate or clone websites and social media profiles to generate what look like genuine official pages and mislead people into thinking they are on authorised platforms. This can lead to victims making fake purchases – paying for goods that do not exist – or sharing their personal details online.
Global Village VIP packs
VIP packs for Global Village went on sale on Saturday. This year, the packs are redesigned around a new 'Global Village storybook' theme. They feature seven collectable pins, alongside a selection of premium Global Village experiences and benefits. One lucky VIP pack holder will get a chance to win Dh31,000 ($8,440).
The Diamond VIP Pack is the most expensive option at Dh7,900, followed by Platinum at Dh3,490, Gold at Dh2,490 and Silver at Dh1,890.
Each pack includes benefits such as a VIP parking sticker, parking cards, a number of entry tickets depending on the tier bought, and Wonder Pass cards with priority access to rides and bonus points when topping up.
Anyone aged 18 or older holding a valid Emirates ID is eligible to purchase.
Mega VIP packs return
Global Village is bringing back its Mega Gold and Mega Silver packs, which combine its VIP benefits with passes or tickets for Dubai Parks and Resorts, which reopens on October 7.
Buyers can choose between three-month multi-park seasonal passes or one-day, two-park tickets.
The Mega Gold pack costs Dh4,990 and includes either eight seasonal passes or 12 park tickets. The Mega Silver costs Dh3,490 and includes either five seasonal passes or seven park tickets.
Both have a Dh150 priority booking fee during the pre-order period.

The U.S. military formally ends a more than two-decade-long presence in Iraq this week.

￼
items.titleTR: After more than two decades, U.S. forces prepare to leave Iraq

items.descriptionTR:
Iraq's Counterterrorism Service (CTS) has killed two suspected ISIS suicide bombers in the northern province of Kirkuk, days before the planned withdrawal of US troops from the country.
The CTS said its forces clashed with three terrorists from the “remnants” of ISIS in the town of Altun Kupri, north of Kirkuk city. Two of them, who were wearing belts laden with explosives, were killed, while their driver was wounded and arrested, the statement added. No details were given about their nationalities.
Maj Gen Saad Maan, spokesman for the Iraqi Security Media Cell, later said a civilian was killed and two CTS members were injured in the clashes on Sunday. The CTS said the operation was carried out in accordance with judicial orders and as part of its continuous security and intelligence efforts to weed out terrorist gangs.
“The Counterterrorism Service confirms the continuation of its qualitative operations to pursue the remnants of terrorism to defend Iraq's security and the safety of its people,” a statement read.
Altun Kupri lies on the road between Kirkuk and Erbil, the capital of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region. Since the territorial defeat of ISIS in Iraq in late 2017, remnants continue to operate in small cells in remote areas, mainly in desert areas or valleys, and it is unusual for clashes with militant fighters to break out in urban areas.
The operation came days before a planned withdrawal of US troops on Wednesday, following the end of the combat mission of the US-led anti-ISIS international coalition in Iraq.
Under an agreement reached in 2024 between Baghdad and Washington, once the coalition's military mission in Iraq concludes it will be followed by a transition to a bilateral security partnership focused on advising, training and intelligence sharing.
US forces have already left several bases in Iraq and will continue to operate with reduced numbers in Kurdistan until September 30 for operations against ISIS in Syria.
￼
The move has sparked a heated political argument inside Iraq.
The government of Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi and its supporters, including the Co-ordination Framework, say Iraqi forces are now capable of maintaining security independently and that ending the foreign combat presence restores full sovereignty. The CF is the largest parliamentarian bloc and consist of Iran-backed political parties and militias.
Opponents, including some Sunni and Kurdish politicians and security analysts, have expressed concerns about the capabilities of Iraqi forces to contain ISIS without coalition air power, intelligence and logistical support.
The group still poses a lethal but low-level threat and that withdrawal could create security gaps, opponents of the coalition withdrawal say, particularly in the rugged and poorly policed areas that are still contested between Baghdad and Erbil, by federal and Kurdish forces.
In 2003, the US led an international coalition to invade Iraq and topple Saddam Hussein’s regime, claiming it was developing and stockpiling weapons of mass destruction. No such weapons were found and the invasion plunged Iraq into years of chaos.
By the end of 2011, the US had withdrawn from Iraq, leaving a small number of troops to protect its embassy, and train and assist Iraqi forces. At its peak in 2007, the US military presence consisted of 170,000 soldiers.
Foreign combat troops returned in 2014, by which time ISIS had seized about a third of the country as the US-trained Iraqi security forces melted away. Then, the Iraqi government asked the US to support it in its fight against ISIS.
In excerpts from an interview with Iraqi TV broadcast on Saturday, Masoud Barzani, the leader of Kurdistan Democratic Party said he feared the “same scenario” of 2014 would develop.
When ISIS arrived in 2014, he said, “the then-Iraqi government solicited the US, European countries and Nato to ‘come and help us’”.
items.titleTR: Iraq counterterror forces kill ISIS fighters ahead of US-led coalition departure

slots.packetSpot:
US forces are expected to formally end their more than 20-year military presence in Iraq this week. While the remaining troops serving as part of the anti-ISIS coalition are expected to leave by Wednesday, the relationship will shift to a bilateral security partnership based on advisory support, training and intelligence sharing.

As this transition continues, Iraq’s Counter Terrorism Service said it had clashed with three people described as ISIS remnants in Altun Kupri near Kirkuk. According to the statement, two suspects wearing explosive belts were killed; their driver was wounded and detained. Saad Maan, spokesperson for Iraq’s Security Media Cell, reported that one civilian was killed in the clash and two Counter Terrorism Service personnel were wounded.

It is reported that since ISIS lost territorial control in Iraq in 2017, it has operated in small cells, mostly in remote areas; clashes inside cities are unusual. While the government and its supporters argue that Iraqi forces are capable of ensuring security on their own, some Sunni and Kurdish politicians and security analysts voice concern that capability gaps could emerge without the coalition’s air support, intelligence and logistics. Kurdistan Democratic Party leader Masoud Barzani also said he was concerned that a situation similar to that of 2014 could develop.

items.descriptionTR:
Jenn Lichter’s childhood followed a difficult path. The resilience she gained helped her achieve an unbreakable ultrarunning feat this summer
On 27 June, Jenn Lichter lined up for her first 100-mile race, the Western States 100. The oldest and most prestigious 100-miler in the world, Western States attracts a highly competitive field from around the globe – the athletes run across the Sierra Nevada from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California. Despite 18,000ft of climbing and daytime temperatures often flirting with triple digits, Lichter went in confident. “I wanted to win, there was no secret to that,” she says. “That’s just who I am.”
The race remained close for the first half, until the 30-year-old made a move on the climb to Devil’s Thumb. The gap grew and at the final aid station, Lichter had a sizable lead over the athlete in second place. A mile from the finish, Nick Cornell, Lichter’s fiance, told her she was just ahead of the course record. “That was the first I had heard about it,” Lichter says. “He knew my competitive side would jump at the challenge.”
items.titleTR: ‘Hardships never last’: Jenn Lichter’s path from Colombian orphanage to ultrarunning records

Major sporting events are not just about opening ceremonies and competition schedules: stadiums need to be tested, transport must function, accommodation must be sufficient, and programmes need to withstand weather conditions.

Patrice Motsepe, president of the Confederation of African Football, called for preparations to be accelerated for Afcon 2027, which Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda will co-host. The tournament is scheduled to begin on 19 June and end on 17 July; stadiums are expected to start being used for testing in about three months. Motsepe said there had been progress at the facilities he inspected in Nairobi, but that some areas remained below the required standard. While stressing that there was no plan for a postponement, Kenya's Sports Minister Salim Mvurya gave assurances that the work would be completed in December.

At the Asian Games in Japan, accommodation, transport and scheduling problems reported by athletes made the pressure on the event's day-to-day operations visible. Cancellations and delays caused by rain also strained the schedule in sports such as tennis, cricket and surfing. The organising committee apologised for accommodation and transport errors, saying that the arrival of about 2,000 additional athletes and officials had stretched resources. No traditional athletes' village had been built for the Games, which were spread across Tokyo and Osaka as well as Nagoya and Aichi.

Washington is also reported to have advocated closing some peacekeeping missions, while supporting operations aligned with its own interests, such as the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, the International Stabilization Force in Gaza and the UN mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which has been in place for 27 years. Reservations over extending the mission in the Central African Republic are also cited as part of this selective approach.

The issues Ronald Lamola pointed to include land reform, Black economic empowerment, expropriation rules and South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. US visa restrictions, tariffs, aid cuts, refugee policy and its stance on the G20 summit to be hosted by the United States are cited among the instruments of disagreement between the two countries; South Africa says it is ready to attend the summit if invited.

In Mexico City, Claudia Sheinbaum also spoke out against intervention, interventionism and violations of her country’s territorial integrity in a speech in Zócalo Square. Her remarks stood out as a message of sovereignty in response to pressure and threats said to have come from the United States under the framework of “combating narco-terrorism.” Both capitals are publicly stressing their determination to preserve their own policy space on contentious issues with Washington.

items.titleTR: Amid changing dynamics in the Middle East, Turkey seeks to emerge as a leader

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Less than two months after his government hosted the NATO summit — which was framed as proof of Turkey’s pivotal role in transatlantic security — President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has proposed full Turkish membership in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, an entity that has been described as being anti-NATO or a “rogue NATO.” The apparent contradiction
items.titleTR: Erdogan playing East and West, winning room to maneuver

slots.packetSpot:
Turkey is preserving its position within NATO while seeking a broader role in the Middle East and trying to expand its room for manoeuvre between different centres of power through its proposal for full membership in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. This orientation is interpreted less as a definitive turn from West to East than as Ankara’s pursuit of greater autonomy across competing strategic spheres.

In this Middle Eastern pursuit, the defence industry, mediation initiatives and cultural influence stand out. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on 7 August is also cited in this context. In Syria, following reports that the Assad regime collapsed in 2024, Turkey is said to have secured reconstruction contracts and taken on a role in rebuilding the army.

The rivalry between Turkey and Israel is said to have become more visible in Syria. Israel said that an attack targeting an unused air base in northern Syria in early August was intended to prevent the deployment of Turkish forces; Turkey rejected this, while US officials described the attack as “unnecessary escalation”. It is emphasised that the sides increasingly view one another through a zero-sum framework, though a possible conflict is not certain.

Ankara’s room for manoeuvre is not unlimited either: its economy remains strongly dependent on European markets and Western financing, while NATO continues to be decisive in security. Russia, China and Iran are partners in some areas and rivals in others; for this reason, multidirectional diplomacy carries both flexibility and the risk of friction.
slots.packetTitle: Ankara between the blocs

items.descriptionTR:
Israel has lashed out at the Netherlands after it banned the import of goods from illegal settlements, the latest in a series of disputes with traditional allies who are growing increasingly vocal in their opposition to Israeli conduct.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announced that Dutch diplomats serving in the Palestinian city of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank have seven days to hand over their Israeli diplomatic credentials.
This will greatly limit their ability to carry out diplomatic work with Palestinians, after the Netherlands reportedly began enforcing a ban on goods from Israeli businesses operating in occupied territories.
“If the Netherlands wishes to continue representing its interests with the Palestinians, it may do so from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the State of Israel,” Mr Saar said in a post on X.
￼
The announcement from Mr Saar came after Dutch customs officers searched the luggage of passengers arriving in Amsterdam on Israeli airline El Al for settlement goods. The Netherlands' policy came into effect last week and does not affect goods purchased within Israel's sovereign borders. Intentional violation of the law could result in up to six years’ in prison.
Israeli news outlet Haaretz reported on Monday that a kosher supermarket in Amsterdam informed customers earlier in the month that a number of products from Israeli settlements would no longer be available on its shelves.
The move marks the latest deterioration in relations with western allies, as momentum grows to act against Israel’s rapidly expanding settler movement, which throws into jeopardy the future of the two-state solution, long regarded by much of the international community as the preferred route to ending the Israel-Palestine conflict.
Since the far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came into power in 2022, Israel's settlement project in the occupied territories has accelerated, alongside a huge rise in settler-related violence against Palestinians. There is also rising criticism of Israeli conduct during the Gaza war.
Territories affected by the Netherlands' ban include the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.
Israel’s revocation of diplomatic privileges comes weeks after it closed the British Consulate in Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, after the UK announced sanctions against occupied West Bank settlements. The move was followed by similar announcements from 11 other western countries.
The spate of punitive measures puts the targeted western diplomats in a complicated position, as they must now decide whether to leave the territory and possibly relocate to a nearby capital such as Amman, or operate with less protection within Jerusalem or the West Bank.
The dilemma is further complicated because much of the international community views East Jerusalem as occupied Palestinian territory under international law, in which Israel does not have the right to expel diplomats, while Israel claims the entirety of Jerusalem is its undivided capital.
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a strong supporter of Israeli settlements, lambasted the “insane” Dutch decision, claiming that buying a “nativity set from Bethlehem could put you in prison”. Bethlehem is a Palestinian city in the West Bank, not an Israeli settlement, so the Dutch ban would not apply to anything purchased there.
The US recognised Jerusalem as Israel’s capital in 2017 and moved the American embassy from Tel Aviv to the city in 2018. It also acknowledged Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, widely considered by the international community to be Syrian territory, in 2019.
Former Israeli ambassador to the US, Michael Oren, said the Dutch policy showed “the Netherlands, the most pro-Nazi western European country during the German Second World War occupation, has fully returned to its anti-Semitic roots and performing selections on Jews”.
￼
He called on Israel to expel the Dutch ambassador in Tel Aviv “at once”.
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said: “The fact that Israelis are landing in the Netherlands and rummaging through their bags to search for and confiscate products from the settlements is a diplomatic failure unlike anything that has ever happened before.”
Mr Lapid listed other moments such as a plane from Israel reportedly being denied permission to land by authorities in Mauritius last week, the mass walkout of UN delegates during Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech to the General Assembly in New York last week and even recent controversy involving the British singer Ed Sheeran.
“With the right diplomatic work, with the right public diplomacy management, it is possible to stop the anti-Israel wave and return us to being a beloved country in the world,” Mr Lapid, who is in the midst of an election campaign, concluded in a post on X. “This won't happen with this government. The fix will begin in another month,” he added.

There are also differing calculations regarding the cost of the Chagos agreement: while the British government puts its net present value at £3.4 billion, the Conservative opposition calculates the nominal total at £34.7 billion; another measure puts the amount at around £10 billion. items.descriptionTR:
The Nepali government has requested $20m from the UN fund for “loss and damage”, following the devastating floods that hit…
The post Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs appeared first on Carbon Brief.
Print article Share

Article Contents
Expand menu
The Nepali government has requested $20m from the UN fund for “loss and damage”, following the devastating floods that hit the country in late August.
This amounts to just 0.7% of the $2.7bn it has estimated in “physical damage” to infrastructure and “economic losses” from the flooding, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
The $20m request would, nevertheless, make Nepal the fourth-largest claimant to the UN loss-and-damage fund, which is intended to help deal with climate-related disasters.
Developing countries have already made 176 applications to the UN fund for responding to loss and damage, requesting, in total, $2.8bn to help recover from a variety of damaging events, such as drought, floods and storms.
Yet, to date, predominantly developed nations have only pledged $0.8bn to support the fund.
This means requests to the fund are already three times larger than the total amount pledged, raising questions about its potential to respond to emergencies.
As yet, no funding has been paid out of the fund to developing countries grappling with intensifying and more frequent climate change-induced disasters since it was established in 2023.
Nepal’s needs
On 26 August, Nepal was hit by flash floods following a catastrophic rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayan border region. The flooding has killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. 
Days later, the Nepali government sought an “urgent response” from the board of the UN fund for climate-driven loss and damage. 
It subsequently requested $20m in “financial compensation” from the fund. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project.
“Loss and damage” is a term used to describe how climate change is causing serious and, in many cases, irreversible impacts around the world. Nations established the UN fund in 2023, after decades of effort by climate-vulnerable nations.
Nepal’s national disaster management authority has now released an extensive rapid preliminary assessment of “damage and needs” from the floods.
￼
As the chart below shows, Nepal’s $20m loss-and-damage claim would only cover 0.7% of what authorities describe as $2.7bn in “total damage and loss” from the floods.
When accounting for another $4.8bn in “recovery and reconstruction” costs – part of how loss and damage is internationally defined – then Nepal’s $20m claim would be just 0.3% of the needs it estimates.  Reacting to the analysis, Nepal’s climate negotiator Raju Pandit Chhetri tells Carbon Brief that the country’s $20m request was for “rapid response”, adding: 
“That money is going to be a peanut if it was to be invested into reconstruction.”
Requests vs pledges
Vulnerable, developing countries have long argued that developed nations should be held responsible for loss and damage, while countries such as the US have blocked moves that could have led to them being liable for climate-related damages
From December 2025 until July 2026, developing countries made 176 applications to the loss-and-damage fund, requesting over $2.8bn in assistance.
So far, predominantly developed countries have pledged only $822m to the fund. (Some nations that are not categorised as “developed” under the UN, such as the UAE and South Korea, have also committed funds.)
Funding requests from developing countries to date are, therefore, more than triple what has been pledged.
￼
Apart from Nepal’s new request, “requested” data is based on the project pipeline as of 29 June 2026. Analysis by Carbon Brief.
Moreover, only around half of the money pledged so far has been paid into the fund by donor nations, with large sums from France, Italy and the UAE still outstanding.
The fund has made $342m available in its initial funding round in July 2026. However, as of September, no money from the fund has been distributed to any countries facing climate-related disasters.

￼

According to Carbon Brief analysis, off the 176 loss-and-damage fund requests received from 118 countries, more than 60% are from least developed countries  – such as Nepal – and small-island nations. So far, each individual funding request is capped at $20m. 
The flood-related request is Nepal’s fourth appeal to the fund and, as the chart below shows, this makes it the fourth-largest claimant overall. 
￼
Apart from Nepal’s new request, data is based on the project pipeline as of 29 June 2026. Analysis by Carbon Brief.
Nine other countries have made multiple requests to the fund. Madagascar – hit by back-to-back cyclones after a prolonged drought – has made six requests in total. 
Drought-ravaged Suriname, Ecuador, Brazil and Barbados have specified that their funding requests are part of an “emergency response”.
‘Rapid response’
Nepal’s $20m claim has sparked a conversation on climate justice and the ability of the loss-and-damage fund to deliver, in the face of increasingly frequent extreme-weather events.
In a letter sent five days after the disaster, Nepal’s finance minister Dr Swarnim Wagle appealed to the fund’s board to mobilise an “urgent response” that would “signal” that the fund:
“[I]s capable of responding with humanity, speed, flexibility and solidarity when climate-vulnerable countries face losses and damages beyond their capacity to address alone.”
￼
Board members from Asia-Pacific and African countries wrote a letter in support of the Himalayan country in crisis, urging the board to convene and “potentially agree to a provisional set-aside allocation of resources to support rapid response funding for Nepal”. 
They pointed out that the board’s response to Nepal could offer “procedural lessons” in how to strengthen its “rapid-response” to sudden-onset extreme-weather events. Such support is explicitly part of the fund’s mandate.
On 14 September, developed-country members of the fund’s board wrote that they supported a “consultation” on Nepal, but made no commitments in terms of actual funding. 
Harjeet Singh, loss-and-damage expert and global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, tells Carbon Brief that the fund’s board deals with most funding requests as regular projects, rather than emergencies. Singh continues: 
“Developed countries gave a really cold response to Nepal’s request. They have not addressed it because they know that if this happens once, they are going to be under pressure all the time. This is unacceptable.” 
Meanwhile, BBC News reported that Nepal plans to use climate attribution studies to strengthen its claim.
According to a rapid attribution study by World Weather Attribution and climate experts who spoke to Carbon Brief, factors such as glacial retreat and permafrost thaw that played a key role in the disaster have been linked to climate change. A full attribution study is pending. 
Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah will address the UN general assembly on 24 September and is expected to raise issues around climate justice, loss and damage and the vulnerability of mountain countries.  The next board meeting of the loss and damage fund is on 15 December, two months from now, and a fortnight after the conclusion of COP31 in Turkey.
Pandit Chhetri tells Carbon Brief:
“It’s a shame that, until now, the fund has not been able to even give a penny to developing countries. And, starkly, the event in Nepal only demonstrates why this kind of fund is so important for highly vulnerable, poor, developing countries.”
Pandit Chhetri adds that, after nearly three weeks since the disaster, there is yet to be a decision on the request and that the country has “only received messages of solidarity”, with no assurance of rapid response funds. He says that it is “quite an interesting scene for [us] to observe”, adding:
“If the fund cannot respond in a crisis like this for a country like Nepal – when you have this massive destruction and devastation – then what is the use of the fund itself? That’s why it is a test for the fund, though the resources are limited.”
