items.descriptionTR:
In the coming months, the world will get a glimpse of life on an even hotter planet.
By now, you’ve seen the headlines, and there’s more of them every day: It’s “jaw-dropping.” It’s poised to make global warming worse. California has just declared a statewide state of emergency. This year’s El Niño — a shift in Pacific Ocean trade winds that scrambles global weather patterns — has been hotly discussed as one of the strongest on record, and one that could bring about potentially disastrous consequences. One study projects that it may cause as many as 451,000 heat-related deaths around the world by February.  
The current El Niño has also been given an array of eye-catching descriptors. When Jeffrey Shaman, a climatologist at Columbia Climate School, heard the phrase “super El Niño” for the first time earlier this year, he said, “I literally googled it.” The phrase isn’t officially used by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration or the World Meteorological Organization. But he still sees value in the label as a way of communicating the significance of this year’s likely unprecedented El Niño to the general public. 
“It’s colloquial, and there’s nothing wrong with that at all,” Shaman said. 
By all accounts, this year’s El Niño will also give the world a glimpse into a future of unabated warming due to the burning of fossil fuels — and an opportunity to change course before the worst effects occur.
￼
People wade through a flooded road caused by monsoon rains in Apalit, Pampanga, Philippines, on August 20.
Daniel Ceng / Anadolu via Getty Images
￼
Water buffaloes emerge from the remaining water in a dried-up lake in Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka, on September 4. El Niño is worsening the drying of lakes and other water sources amid an ongoing drought. 
Thilina Kaluthotage / NurPhoto via Getty Images
Back up — what is El Niño?
El Niño is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon that begins when sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean rise above average. Although it doesn’t occur on a set timeframe, it tends to happen every two to seven years. Typically, trade winds blow east to west across the Pacific and push warm ocean water along the equator toward East Asia. But during an El Niño year, these winds slow down and sometimes reverse. The warm water that typically gets dragged westward sloshes back, now toward the western coast of the Americas. 
This change in sea surface temperatures has ramifications far beyond the Pacific. It drives extreme weather across the globe, threatening crop harvests in several key agricultural regions, as well as worsening both drought and severe rainfall. 
The impact of climate change on El Niño is complex. Research has shown that global warming has led to more frequent El Niños. But El Niño events are also associated with jumps in global mean surface temperature — or the average temperature of the Earth itself, a measure commonly used as a stand-in for climate change. It’s not easy to delineate how much additional warming is from El Niño and how much is from climate change, but what is clear is that the combination will be devastating. This year may turn out to be the hottest year on record, and 2027 may be even hotter. It could be a preview of the typical levels of warming the world might see by 2040, according to one high-end estimate.
Scientists don’t know exactly how that combination will play out. “It’s going to be a very, very strong event occurring against a backdrop of very rapid global warming,” said Christopher Callahan, a climate scientist at Indiana University. “I think we’re going to, unfortunately, learn a lot this year,” he said.
￼
A firefighter in Indonesia tries to extinguish wildfires at Sungai Rambutan Regency in Ogan Ilir, South Sumatera, on September 12. El Niño conditions are helping to fuel wildfires across the country. 
Muhammad Fajri / Anadolu via Getty Images
￼
Francisco Molina shows corn kernels that failed to germinate at the village of Los Piches in Honduras on September 4. Locals say the drought is one of the worst they can remember, attributing its severity to the powerful El Niño weather pattern. 
Orlando Sierra / AFP via Getty Images
What makes this El Niño ‘super’?
There are many ways to measure the strength of an El Niño event. (NOAA keeps track of several of them here.) Some measure the sea surface temperature in different regions of the Pacific; there’s also indexes that take into account atmospheric changes as well as oceanic ones. The one used most often today is called the “Niño 3.4 anomaly.” In the U.S., in order for NOAA to declare an El Niño event, warming in this region of the Pacific must be 0.5 degrees Celsius above normal. If warming is 1 degree above normal, that gets labeled as “moderate”; if it’s 1.5 degrees above normal, then it counts as “strong”; and if it’s 2 degrees above normal, then it’s considered “very strong.”
The term “super” is broadly considered to be synonymous with “very strong.” However, a recent analysis of sea surface temperatures by Carbon Brief, released this week, shows that as of Monday, warming in the Niño 3.4 region reached 3.11 degrees.
That number is significant, because it means this year’s El Niño has already broken the record for the strongest El Niño, which peaked in November 2015. 
El Niño events typically peak around December or January. (Fun fact: The phenomenon was named El Niño by South American fishers who noticed its timing and associated the warmer temperatures with the story of baby Jesus.) It’s possible that sea surface temperatures in the Pacific will drop over the next few months. However, that looks increasingly unlikely. Sea surface temperatures in June, July, and August were the warmest we’ve ever seen, and forecast models show that there is now a 90 percent chance that this El Niño will stay “very strong” through the end of the year. 
“I was a little bit skeptical earlier this year of some of the more dire predictions,” said Callahan. But as more data kept coming in, he said, it became clear “that we’re going to see a generationally strong event this year.”
￼
A worker monitors wind speed and direction in the Pacific at the Peruvian National Emergency Operations Center as part of national multi-hazard drills in preparation for the arrival of El Niño. Carlos Garcia Granthon/ Fotoholica Press / LightRocket via Getty Images
￼
Workers secure a container ship as it passes through the Cocoli Locks of the Panama Canal on September 3 ahead of reduced transit measures linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon.
Martin Bernetti / AFP via Getty Images
Where did the phrase ‘super El Niño’ come from?
While it might sound like a phrase an overzealous journalist invented, “super El Niño” was actually coined by scientists — a fact that surprised Jovana Vurdelja, an ecolinguistics researcher in Serbia. “I really thought it was just media sensationalism,” she said. The phrase first appeared in a 2003 paper looking at how a strong El Niño can be followed by a strong La Niña, its cooler counterpart, according to Vurdelja.
“Super El Niño” has taken off in English-speaking countries but also across Europe, where it’s been adopted by speakers of Serbian, Norwegian, Italian, German, French, Croatian, and other languages. 
When extraordinary weather is on the way, people reach for amped-up language to communicate the scale of the hazard. But finding the right word to match that danger is like trying to find the right shoe size, Vurdelja said. The language can be too small, minimizing the threat, or it can be too big — exaggerations that can lead to nihilism or desensitization. “It’s extremely important that the word communicates the seriousness, the magnitude, the severity of the event itself,” Vurdelja said. She thinks “super El Niño” hits the mark, since it’s been embraced by scientists and the media alike.
￼
A boy plays in the water of a public fountain as he cools off amid high temperatures linked to the El Nino weather phenomenon in Cali, Colombia, on September 23. 
Joaquin Sarimiento / AFP via Getty Images
￼
Crews work along the Southern California shoreline on September 15. A strengthening El Niño is worsening coastal erosion, threatening homes in Dana Point, California, where several were red-tagged after powerful waves associated with Hurricane Marie battered the coastline.
Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
What comes after ‘super El Niño’?
If super El Niños become a common occurrence — that is, if warming in the Pacific regularly reaches 3 or more degrees above normal — the language we use to describe these events may need to evolve. Some scientists have already suggested that the phrase du jour doesn’t go far enough: “This is going to be so far beyond a super El Niño, if the models are right, that we sort of need a new term for it,” the climate scientist Zeke Hausfather said in the podcast Shift Key last month.
We’ll “need stronger words, stronger language, and that’s when we get into this spiral,” Vurdelja said. That’s how you end up with scientists reaching for words like “mind-bogglingly crazy” and “gobsmackingly bananas” (a phrase Hausfather coined) to describe record heat. The term “Godzilla” El Niño, now taking off in news headlines, was coined by NASA climate scientist Bill Patzert in 2015. 
The official categories for what counts as a strong El Niño used to make sense. “We hadn’t gotten above 2 degrees Celsius except occasionally,” Shaman said, and so the language experts initially settled on “seemed like a reasonable place to be.”
Whatever you call it, the most important thing will be planning for the potential impacts of this very strong El Niño — to understand what it means for food production, hydropower generation, public health, and extreme weather in the coming year. Given California’s recent state of emergency declaration, for now, maybe “super” will do just fine.
This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Whether it’s ‘super’ or ‘Godzilla,’ El Niño is already breaking records on Sep 25, 2026.

items.titleTR: Why is this monster El Niño so strong?

items.descriptionTR:
Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice
Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.
The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.
items.titleTR: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial

slots.packetSpot:
El Niño appears to have reached record levels in some measurements even before peaking. In Carbon Brief’s analysis, warming in the Niño 3.4 region reached 3.11°C; this exceeded the previous strongest El Niño peak in 2015. Although labels such as “super” and “Godzilla” have become widespread, these are not official classifications of NOAA or the World Meteorological Organization.

Forecasts put the likelihood that very strong conditions will persist until the end of 2026 at 90 percent. Models presented by Azhar Ehsan of Columbia University and the assessment by NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center see it as almost certain that the event will continue for about another six months, until spring 2027; its intensity is then expected to decline.

Behind this unusual strength, warm water accumulated in the western Pacific under previous La Niña conditions, strong eastward wind bursts and the Kelvin waves they generated stand out. According to Michael McPhaden, the thermocline in the eastern Pacific has deepened by more than 80 metres from normal in some places; this makes it harder for cold water to rise to the surface. Whether global warming directly strengthens El Niño remains an open question. By contrast, it is stated that a warmer world could intensify consequences such as drought, extreme rainfall, flooding, fires, heat and coastal impacts.

Risks to hurricane activity, agriculture, food production, hydropower, public health and water resources are on the agenda across a broad geography stretching from the United States to the Philippines, and from Sri Lanka to Indonesia. While the World Food Programme warns that 50 million people could face acute hunger, another estimate suggests that El Niño’s additional heat could lead to 450,000 deaths by February; these are not outcomes that have occurred, but projections.

items.descriptionTR:
An area of Amazon forest roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey has remained standing due to…
The post Analysis: Lula presidency saved at least 20,000km2 of Brazilian Amazon since 2022 appeared first on Carbon Brief.
Print article Share

Article Contents
Expand menu
An area of Amazon forest roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey has remained standing due to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s leadership of Brazil, according to Carbon Brief analysis. 
Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election to become president of the nation that is home to nearly 60% of the Amazon rainforest. 
Forest loss surged during Bolsonaro’s far-right presidency and dropped sharply under the left-wing Lula, with Amazon deforestation likely to hit its lowest level on record this year. 
Now, as another presidential election approaches, Lula is facing off against Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, whose “anti-environmental” policies are similar to his father’s.
Carbon Brief’s analysis suggests that at least 20,000 square kilometres (km2) of deforestation has been avoided since Lula took office and prioritised Amazon protection.
The analysis is based on modelling by an international research team of an alternative scenario in which Brazil’s flagship forest code legislation was not enforced – a proxy for Jair Bolsonaro’s leadership. 
Experts tell Carbon Brief that this estimate is likely “conservative” and that actual deforestation under Bolsonaro could have been “much higher”. 
With Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied in the polls, the upcoming election is expected to significantly shape the level of environmental action in the world’s fourth-largest emitter, whose emissions are largely driven by deforestation. 
‘Brazil is back’
When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil between 2019 and 2022, he championed the nation’s powerful agribusiness sector and oversaw an unprecedented increase in Amazon deforestation.
Bolsonaro weakened regulations, slashed federal agency budgets and empowered illegal activities in the Amazon, while attacking Indigenous and environmental groups.
This meant that the forest code – Brazil’s flagship legislation that requires landowners to preserve and restore forest on their property – was not properly enforced.
After Lula’s presidential victory in 2022, he promised to target “zero deforestation” by 2030, telling the COP27 UN climate summit that “Brazil is back”.
Lula rolled back Bolsonaro’s wave of deregulation and reinstated a deforestation “action plan”. Led by celebrated environmentalist Marina Silva, the environment ministry scaled up enforcement and policing activities in the Amazon. 
As a result, annual deforestation in the Amazon has more than halved from 11,594km2 per year in 2022 to 5,731km2 in 2025.
Data from August 2025 to July 2026 – the timespan used in government records – is yet to be released, but preliminary satellite alerts put the deforestation figure at 2,874km2.
While the final figure is likely to be higher, experts still think Amazon deforestation in 2026 could hit its lowest level since records began in 1988.
New Jersey-sized forest
Compared to a scenario in which Bolsonaro won in 2022, Carbon Brief analysis suggests that at least 20,000km2 of Amazon forest remains standing today due to Lula’s leadership.
This area – roughly the size of Wales, Belize, Slovenia or the US state of New Jersey – is indicated by the grey area in the chart below.
￼
Each year covers a period from August to July. Deforestation data is from INPE’s PRODES dataset, except for the 2026 figure. This is based on INPE’s DETER real-time satellite alert data, which tends to give lower estimates than PRODES. The “Bolsonaro” projections are based on a scenario with no forest code enforcement, from a 2023 study.
This analysis is based on a 2023 study on the role of nature-based solutions in Brazil’s pathway to net-zero emissions. This was a refined update of a 2018 study that used the same GLOBIOM-Brazil model, from researchers at the University of Oxford, the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis and Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research (INPE).
It is based on a comparison of forest code implementation with a “baseline” scenario in which the code is not enforced, reflecting the kind of weak governance seen under the Bolsonaro administration. (See Carbon Brief’s 2022 article for more details of this modelling.)
Dr Aline Soterroni, a University of Oxford researcher who led the 2023 analysis, tells Carbon Brief that the reversal seen under Lula “shows how quickly deforestation can respond to political will”.
However, she stresses that the modelling of the “no forest code” scenario is “relatively conservative”, with deforestation remaining high but not rising. 
Deforestation in this scenario – used here as a proxy for a Bolsonaro election win – is tempered by slower demand growth for Brazilian beef and soy, says Soterroni. She notes that the scenario also does not capture the potential for illegal forest clearing in response to weak governance.
Indeed, some experts anticipated in 2022 that a Bolsonaro victory would send deforestation rates rising to near-record levels.
Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Brazil’s Climate Observatory, tells Carbon Brief that if Bolsonaro had won in 2022, “we have reason to believe [this would have resulted] in much higher rates than during his first term”.
Angelo says the “political signal” would likely have driven an “explosion of wildcat mining” and illegal deforestation in the Amazon. He also points to efforts – including by Flávio Bolsonaro – to formally dismantle the forest code in the Brazilian congress, during Jair Bolsonaro’s first term.
Soterroni notes that deforestation rates did not immediately drop following Lula’s election, as suggested by modelling of a full “forest code compliance” scenario. She says this reflects the “gradual and imperfect process” of restoring and enforcing the law.
Nevertheless, she tells Carbon Brief:
“The key message from our modelling is the contrast between these trajectories: weak environmental governance keeps deforestation substantially higher than full implementation of the forest code. That message remains relevant today.”
Election significance
With Jair Bolsonaro in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, his son Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator for Rio de Janeiro, is standing against Lula in the upcoming contest for president.
There are 13 candidates, but Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula are by far the frontrunners and are currently neck-and-neck in opinion polls. 
If Lula wins, experts say he is likely to continue with the “zero deforestation by 2030” agenda that has already had a pronounced impact on forest loss. 
As the chart below shows, periods when Amazon deforestation fell in recent history all occurred during Lula’s three terms as president. 
￼
In contrast, experts say Flávio Bolsonaro, a climate sceptic who has indicated he will continue his father’s political agenda and favour agribusiness and mining, will likely drive a surge in deforestation. Angelo tells Carbon Brief:
“At the risk of sounding alarmist, I’ve been saying that Lula’s re-election is the only thing standing between us and a wide destruction of the Amazon.”
A Bolsonaro win would be a “tremendous disaster”, says Dr Patricia Pinho, deputy science director at the Amazon Environmental Research Institute, adding: 
“I don’t think we can afford four years of increasing deforestation [and] violence against Indigenous peoples.” 
Dr David Lapola, an ecologist focused on Amazon research at the University of Campinas in Brazil, says he believes deforestation “would certainly rise” and Brazil’s climate and deforestation goals “would be thrown in the trash bin”. He tells Carbon Brief: 
“The Bolsonaro administration in the 2019-2022 period showed that the deconstruction of environmental policies and institutes can be done very, very quickly. 
“In a matter of a few months, they can destroy what has been constructed over decades of environmental policy and activism in Brazil.” 
‘Greenest’ policies 
Lula has the “greenest” policy proposals of Brazil’s six top-polling presidential candidates, according to analysis by the Climate Observatory. 
The analysis identifies 16 “positive and detailed” environmental commitments in Lula’s proposals, including reaffirming his “zero deforestation by 2030” goal. 
Flávio Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has one positive environmental commitment and seven “clearly anti-environmental” proposals. 
The right-wing politician has committed to zero “illegal” deforestation by 2029. However, he has also previously led an attempt to change the forest code, opening up large tracts of previously out-of-bounds forest for legal clearance by extractive industries. 
Given this, Angelo tells Carbon Brief that he is sceptical about the 2029 pledge. 
“The only way you can trust him on this is to think that he is going to revoke the forest code and make all illegal deforestation legal.”
￼
Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro with a cardboard cutout of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo
Lula is also the only major candidate to list a clear target for cutting national emissions, sticking with Brazil’s existing goal to cut emissions by 59-67% by 2035, compared to 2005 levels. 
Overall, the Climate Observatory notes that climate change and environmental issues “are off the radar for most candidates”, who are instead focusing on the economy and security issues. 
Pinho adds that deforestation and the Amazon have not been at the “forefront” of this election, compared to 2022. 
If Bolsonaro wins, up to 95% of the Amazon would fall under the leadership of right-wing national governments – including those in Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru – reported Mongabay. It noted that presidents in all these nations “explicitly favour agribusiness and mining over environmental conservation”.
If no candidate receives a majority of votes in the first round of Brazil’s election on 4 October, a runoff will take place on 25 October, as has happened at every presidential election since 1998.
Soy moratorium and Brazilian congress
Other factors will also play a role in future deforestation in Brazil, regardless of the next president. 
One is the effective end of the Amazon soy moratorium. This is a voluntary agreement signed by companies committing to not buy soya beans grown on land in the Brazilian Amazon that was deforested after 2008. 
Conservation organisation WWF’s international director general, Kirsten Schuijt, previously described it as the “most impactful voluntary supply chain policy ever implemented”. 
However, major grain traders withdrew from the agreement earlier this year, effectively bringing it to an end. Pinho describes this move as a “huge destruction” of Brazil’s environmental protections. 
Research shows the moratorium prevented around 18,000km2 of deforestation in its first decade of operation from 2005-16. 
In contrast, a 2026 study estimated that the end of the moratorium could result in 14,000km2 of additional deforestation in the Amazon by 2036. 
Alongside choosing a new president on 4 October, Brazilian voters will elect state governors and members of congress, which will also factor into future environmental impacts.
Right-leaning parties, including the far-right Liberal Party linked to the Bolsonaros, currently hold half the seats of the two chambers of congress. 
This has led to conflict between lawmakers and Lula. For example, in 2025, congress bypassed Lula’s veto of several aspects of a controversial piece of legislation dubbed the “devastation bill”. 
Pinho says that the potential for a right-wing congress and president would be “devastating for the environmental and climate agenda”. 
Lapola notes that a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency “would consolidate the view in Brazil that environmental protection is solely a matter of political preference, and not a crucial need of all people”. He adds: 
“Land pillage, destruction of precious biodiversity and scorning of Indigenous peoples simply cannot be a nation’s project in the 21st century. We have got to be smarter than that, for sure.”

items.titleTR: Analysis: Lula presidency saved at least 20,000km2 of Brazilian Amazon since 2022

items.descriptionTR: As Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeks a fourth term as Brazil's president, he claims to have strengthened protections for the Amazon. However, his support for new oil exploration is clouding his image as an environmental defender.
items.titleTR: Lula's mixed environmental record has brought less deforestation but more oil

slots.packetSpot:
Lula's environmental record presents a picture in which the decline in deforestation in the Amazon sits alongside support for oil exploration. Carbon Brief's modelling suggests that at least 20,000 square kilometres of forest have remained standing since 2023 compared with a scenario assuming weak enforcement of forest laws; this is not an independently measured amount of “saved forest”. The fall in annual loss in INPE data from 11,594 square kilometres in 2022 to 5,731 square kilometres in 2025 is linked to inspection and conservation policies strengthened again under Lula.

Lula advocates a goal of zero deforestation by 2030. However, the continuation of oil exploration makes it difficult to turn this progress in climate and environmental policy into a one-directional narrative of success.
slots.packetTitle: A crack in Lula's green ledger

items.descriptionTR:
If you could look down at the Pacific Ocean right now, you’d see three hurricanes spinning in a row, between 15 and 20 degrees north. Furthest east is Polo, an unusually strong hurricane that has been churning off the southern coast of Mexico for nearly a week. To its west, Odalys, once a Category 4 hurricane, is slowly weakening in the open ocean. In the central Pacific, Hurricane Nolo has reached Category 2 status and has crept about 145 miles off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, where it’s expected to bring up to 25 inches of rain, potentially causing flooding and landslides. The ocean is a mess of hurricanes, and it’s not the first time this season.

Just last month, four storms formed across the Pacific over a 12-day period. Two of them, Hurricane Lala and Tropical Storm Moke, came dangerously close to Hawaii. Driven by an exceptional El Niño event, these tropical storms have increased in frequency compared with an average year. Typically, at this point in the season, 12 tropical storms would have formed in the eastern Pacific, Michael Brennan, the director of the National Hurricane Center, told me. This year, there have already been 17.

Of the storms in the Pacific now, Polo, which has wobbled between Category 4 and 5, is the monster, and it will likely bring catastrophic damage when it makes landfall on Monday. The warm water temperatures associated with El Niño increase the likelihood of stronger storms, and this year’s event is shaping up to be one of the most dramatic on record. “El Niño is the ‘great nudger’ of weather systems around the planet,” Michelle L’Heureux, who leads the El Niño–Southern Oscillation team at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center, wrote in an email. “Very strong El Niños are often able to nudge more.”

Warmer waters also mean that the area where a storm can form expands. Storms tend to show up in the region where Polo is lingering, Brennan said, and generally, by the time they reach the central part of the ocean, near Hawaii, they weaken. But this year, waters in the central Pacific are more than 3 degrees Celsius warmer than usual, allowing hurricanes such as Nolo to form south of the islands and much closer to them. When I asked Brennan how abnormal this was—I’d seen others calling this a historic hurricane season—he said that a season like this comes around every decade or so. Still, it’s a big one.
Nolo is only the latest in a string of disasters that the island of Hawaii has endured this year. In January, the Kilauea volcano erupted for eight hours, and blanketed communities on the island with rocks and ash. Then, back-to-back Kona lows, a type of seasonal cyclone, brought historic flooding in March. Two months later, a 6.0-magnitude earthquake shook the island and damaged nearly 150 homes. In mid-August, Hurricane Lala, a Category 1 storm, dumped some 30 inches of rain on parts of the Big Island without making landfall.

David Ho, a professor of oceanography at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, was at home in Honolulu when Lala hit. His neighborhood flooded, and he was one of 200,000 electricity customers across the state who lost power. More than 200 homes and an estimated $67 million worth of public infrastructure were damaged, according to the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency. “We have a lot of houses that were built before the building codes were modernized,” Ho told me. “So once in a while, you have roofs that just fly away.”

Weeks later, many people, especially those in rural areas with limited access to groceries, are still feeling Lala’s lingering effects. “We always talk about the importance of being prepared, and you want to have three weeks of food supply and everything,” Janice Ikeda, the CEO of the nonprofit Vibrant Hawaii, told me. “Well, we don’t have that anymore, because it got wiped out.” (The state reissued Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits to more than 65,000 households after the storm.) The damage and losses the island suffered from Lala only make lives and infrastructure more vulnerable in the face of Nolo.

For even one storm to skirt that close to Hawaii would have been an event: The Pacific Ocean is big enough, and the Hawaiian Islands are small enough, that most hurricanes roll by at a much greater distance. But earlier this month, another storm, Lowell, approached the western part of the state, near Kauai and Niihau, pushing hurricane-strength winds and waves ashore. More than 90 percent of utility customers in Kauai lost power.

Nolo likely won’t be a repeat of Lala or Lowell, because it is farther out and should remain 100 miles from the coast, Brennan said. Even so, the island could see more than two feet of rain, coastal flooding, and high surf. The hurricane season doesn’t end for another two months, and the effect of El Niño is likely to only get stronger, according to NOAA’s current predictions. Before the year is through, the “great nudger” will likely hurl more hurricanes Hawaii’s way.

In the Atlantic, the nudge is working in the opposite direction: El Niño generates strong wind shears, which make it hard for hurricanes to form. September should mark the peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, Allison Wing, an associate professor of atmospheric science at Florida State University, told me. Nearly four months into hurricane season, no hurricanes have appeared, and none are on the horizon.
Hawaii is on its third close call this season.
items.titleTR: The Pacific Is a Mess of Hurricanes

items.descriptionTR: ￼ Hurricane Nolo strengthened Sunday afternoon as it moved westward south of the Hawaiian Islands, the National Hurricane Center said.
items.titleTR: Category 4 Hurricane Nolo strengthens well southwest of Hawaii

slots.packetSpot:
At a time when three hurricanes are active simultaneously in the Pacific, Nolo stands out as the latest in a succession of close passes near Hawaii. According to the National Hurricane Center’s September 28 update, Nolo, which reached Category 4, was about 420 miles southwest of Honolulu; while it was expected to remain west and southwest of the main Hawaiian Islands, a hurricane warning was in effect for parts of Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument. Dangerous surf and rip current conditions were expected along southern shores.

Earlier assessments had reported that Nolo came within about 145 miles of the Big Island and reached Category 2, bringing risks of heavy rainfall, flooding and landslides. Over the season, Lala, Moke and Lowell also approached Hawaii; it was reported that effects continued in some areas after rainfall, power outages and damage caused by Lala.

National Hurricane Center Director Michael Brennan said 17 tropical storms had formed in the eastern Pacific at this stage, rather than the usual 12. Michelle L’Heureux of NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said strong El Niño conditions can have a greater effect on weather systems; waters in the central Pacific more than 3 degrees Celsius above normal are also conducive to storms forming closer to Hawaii.

items.descriptionTR:
The American farmer, novelist and poet Wendell Berry, died on August 31 2026, aged 92. Berry farmed in Port Royal, in his native Kentucky, for over 40 years. Through his writing and his farming, Berry emphasised the importance of both community and care for the planet, advocating for small-scale agriculture as key for both.
He criticised modern consumer culture, suggesting, in his poem Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front, that instead of buying into the rat race, people should: “Love the world. Work for nothing […] / Say that your main crop is the forests / that you did not plant / that you will not live to harvest.”
His prolific output included The Unsettling of America: Culture and Agriculture (1977), Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer (1987) and The Mad Farmer Poems (2008).
Caring for the planet, Berry believed, means recognising your own place in it. Not as the centre, but as part of a wider community of interconnected life. In doing so, Berry’s writing highlights an important new theme in environmental humanities: a growing interest in “georgic” writing as an environmental genre.
The Peace of Wild Things by Wendell Berry.
The georgic is a classical genre that gets its name from Virgil’s Georgics – a long, four-book poem offering farming advice on ploughing, animal husbandry, fruit growing and beekeeping that was written around 29BC.
While for centuries the georgic was as popular as other classical modes like the pastoral or the epic, by the late 18th-century the form in English had all but disappeared, as the developing science of agriculture became more suited to prose treatises than long, complex poems.
Farming and environmentalism have long been pitched against each other. Over the 20th century, the worst excesses of industrial farming have decimated insect life in the US, as attested to by Rachel Carson’s environmental science book Silent Spring, as well as declining bird life in the UK.
Intensive agriculture has cleared vast swathes of the Amazon rainforest in Brazil and has been linked with the spread of diseases between animals, as well as contributing to antimicrobial resistance and greenhouse gas emissions.
However, since the 1980s, interest has been growing in agroecology and regenerative farming – practices which balance human and environmental needs. Often small-scale and community-led, these practices offer an alternative way of engaging in food production, with projects flourishing from Berry’s native US to Brazil, Spain, Australia and beyond.
In the UK, farmers are increasingly being encouraged to “farm for nature”, with grants available such as the Landscape Recovery scheme, the Sustainable Farming Incentive and the Countryside Stewardship scheme.
The georgic resurgence
This growing interest in balancing agriculture and the natural world is reflected in contemporary books and culture. In the last five years, there has been a growing academic interest in the ways that contemporary georgic writing might respond to environmental concerns.
The resurgence of georgic is in part due to a reimagining of what the form might be. It’s no longer just long, instructional poems that can be thought of as georgic.
Alongside farming novels such as Addlands by Tom Bullough (2017), or The Long Dry (2014) by Cyan Jones, poet Terry Gifford has identified three types of contemporary georgic non-fiction. These include “traditional instructional georgic”, like gardening manuals or the TV programme Countryfile, as well as memoirs, such as The Cow Book: A Story of Life on an Irish Family Farm by John Connell (2019). Finally, there is the genre of rewilding books, such as Wilding by Isabella Tree (2018), which Gifford terms as “radically future-oriented georgic”.
An interview with Wendell Berry.
Environmental humanities scholar Pippa Marland, meanwhile, has identified the “new georgic” – a genre in which farmers are engaged in producing nature itself. She cites English Pastoral by James Rebanks (2021) as a prime example.
While the term “eco-georgic” was only coined in 2011, Wendell Berry’s lifelong commitment to farming for nature and communities and to sharing his ethos and experience through writing, make him a fundamentally eco-georgic figure.
Berry’s legacy
Georgic is a didactic genre: it teaches readers things. Berry can be thought of as a georgic writer not because he wrote how-to manuals on ploughing, beekeeping or fruit-grafting (although he was a contributing editor at both New Farm Magazine and Organic Gardening and Farming), but because there is a fundamental quality about his work that seeks to teach readers how to coexist with nature and care for our planet, while feeding our communities.
In his poem Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front (1973), Berry asks readers to imagine our true crop as the trees that came before us and will outlive us. He urges us to think across the longer span of centuries. In doing so, he asks us to reorient our relationship with the earth. We should not see it simply as something to exploit and profit from. Instead, we should treasure it, even as we enjoy the crops and fruits that sustain us. Every reader, farmers and non-farmers alike, can learn from his broader ethics of care, attention and negotiation with the natural world.
Wendell Berry’s essay Think Little read by Nick Offerman.
Berry’s legacy, then, reflects a growing interest in agroecology over the past decades. But alongside his environmentally conscious farming, his writing touched many, feeding an appetite for ideas about how to live alongside nature, as much as for the food that farming produces.
The flourishing of the eco-georgic genre over the past decade testifies to a continuing and growing interest from readers and writers in a way of farming and living that cares for both nature and communities. Communicating these ideas is as vital as putting them into practice: making the pen is as mighty as the plough.
This article features references to books that have been included for editorial reasons, and may contain links to bookshop.org. If you click on one of the links and go on to buy something, The Conversation UK may earn a commission.
The climate crisis has a communications problem. How do we tell stories that move people – not just to fear the future, but to imagine and build a better one? This article is part of Climate Storytelling, a series exploring how arts and science can join forces to spark understanding, hope and action.

￼
Hannah Green does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Caring for this planet entails decisions that are intimate, about our farms, our homes, our human and our wild neighbours
- by Craig Maier
Read on Aeon
items.titleTR: Where a land ethic blooms

slots.packetSpot:
Wendell Berry’s legacy as a writer and farmer invites us to think of care for the land together with community life. The decisions Craig Maier recounts from his family farm in southern Wisconsin show that this invitation is not an abstract principle: choosing not to cultivate an erosion-prone slope, leaving a grass strip along a stream bank, or returning animal manure to the soil’s cycle emerge as choices that take account of both livelihood and the health of the land.

In this approach, the farm is not merely a place where crops are produced; it is a living environment in which soil organisms, water, animals, plants and human labour are interconnected. Berry’s emphasis on small-scale farming, community and care for the natural world stands alongside approaches under discussion such as agroecology, regenerative agriculture, rewilding and “farming for nature.”

In Maier’s essay, Aldo Leopold’s land ethic is treated not as a one-time principle but as a responsibility renewed through labour, observation and conversation within families and communities. While it is argued that the goal of cheap food and competitive market conditions bind farmers to particular forms of production, it is suggested that turning towards local food and energy production could establish more diverse agricultural and ecological relationships. Care for human neighbours and wildlife emerges here as the long-term reckoning of sharing the same land.
slots.packetTitle: Living beside the land

items.descriptionTR:
Two women and a child have died trying to cross the English Channel after a mega-dinghy capsized off the coast of northern France.
According to the Pas-de-Calais prefecture, there were 105 people on board the vessel, which it described as a “water taxi”, when it capsized at around 10.30am local time on Monday.
“The situation is being assessed and remains subject to change. State services and rescue teams are fully mobilised,” the authority said in a statement.
Some passengers called the emergency services asking to be rescued and were being looked after, according to the Maritime Prefecture of the English Channel and the North Sea.
A rescue ship arrived in the port of Calais midmorning, from which people began to disembark.
So far this year, 22 people are known to have died while attempting to cross the English Channel from France to the UK, official data shows.
The latest incident comes as the UK government is set to open a new legal route for refugees that prioritises Afghan women and girls, and Palestinians.
British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is also set to announce the revival of the UK resettlement scheme, which has been suspended since 2021.
items.titleTR: Two women and a child die after mega-dinghy capsizes in English Channel

slots.packetSpot: According to French authorities, a 10-year-old child and two women in their 30s died on a boat carrying 105 people attempting to cross to the United Kingdom. The boat reportedly ran into difficulty after leaving Blériot Plage in Sangatte, while the exact cause of the deaths is under investigation; initial findings point to crushing.
slots.packetTitle: Three lives in the Channel

superPackets.body:
According to a Carbon Brief analysis, the temperature anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region reached 3.11°C, surpassing the November 2015 peak; El País reported that temperatures in the tropical Pacific were at record levels, while the WMO said it expected the event to peak at the end of the year. While the WMO described conditions as “very strong,” models assigned a 90 percent probability that the event would remain at that level through the end of the year; models cited by The Hill considered it almost certain that El Niño would extend into spring 2027, while Climate Home News wrote that, if the current trajectory is maintained, it could be the strongest in the WMO’s 40-year monitoring period.

Climate Impact Lab combined temperature projections with mortality-rate studies across 24,378 regions to project 451,000 additional heat deaths worldwide between September 2026 and February 2027; the comparison baseline was the 1996-2025 average for the same months. The team projected a combined 66,800 additional deaths for Nigeria, Sudan, Niger and Chad—31,400, 17,500, 10,000 and 8,000 deaths respectively—and identified the Sahel as the region expected to suffer the heaviest losses. The study did not directly examine which populations within countries would be most affected; the figures reported as “tens of thousands” by Mail & Guardian, approximately 450,000 by the Guardian, and 451,000 by Grist were not deaths that had occurred, but projections for the same risk period.

On food, UK climate minister Katie White said that El Niño-linked extreme weather could damage harvests worldwide; the World Food Programme estimate cited by the Guardian was that 50 million people could be pushed into acute hunger, but no geography, period or comparison baseline was specified. According to the FAO’s analysis of 41 years of satellite observations, the likelihood of agricultural drought in some cropland and pasture areas of Central America’s Dry Corridor exceeds 50 percent in the coming months; about half of the region’s 1.9 million farmers producing maize, beans and other staple grains live there. In the United Kingdom, Rebalance Earth reported that 81 percent of fresh produce is already concentrated in areas experiencing water stress; in Limpopo, farmers described farms where production had been abandoned because of erratic rainfall and access to water, but neither record was linked to El Niño. For South Africa, Daily Maverick recorded concerns about the coming season’s harvest and commodity prices; no source measured an actual national harvest loss for this season.

superPackets.body: As Trump and Xi conveyed messages of harmony and non-conflict at the Washington summit, reports wrote that trade and artificial intelligence were discussed, while Taiwan was not mentioned in public statements but was addressed in the private meeting. Euronews stated that important details had not yet been disclosed, the BBC noted that gaps remained regarding what was said and agreed, and the Guardian said that no resolution had emerged on deep-rooted disagreements. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the two governments had agreed to establish an official artificial intelligence dialogue and incident-reporting hotline; writers in The Conversation framed this as a starting point for cooperation after the summit and an arrangement that would be tested through implementation. Two giant pandas named Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, under an intergovernmental lending agreement announced by Xi during the visit, arrived in Atlanta on Sunday; the Guardian counted this as one of the visit's few concrete outcomes. While the Chinese side highlighted Xi's statement that “the Thucydides Trap can be overcome” and messages of goodwill, Trump described the visit as “great”; commentators in The Atlantic, meanwhile, recorded Trump's search for a quick deal and China's approach of gradually easing the relationship as distinct frameworks. Sources did not record how the artificial intelligence channel would operate, what was said in the private meeting on Taiwan, or whether the summit produced a measurable change in other U.S.–China disputes.

superPackets.body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said they had presented a seven-day roadmap for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the start of broader negotiations, that the conditions had been conveyed to Washington through Qatar, and that only a negotiated solution could end the war. Donald Trump announced that he had rejected the proposal; U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said Trump did not trust that Iran was acting in good faith or that it would genuinely negotiate over its nuclear program. No agreement emerged on next steps after three hours of contacts in New York; meanwhile, Araghchi said they were awaiting the final U.S. position from mediators, while an official briefed on the talks told Reuters that Qatar was planning separate contacts with the parties. The National News, CNBC and UPI linked Monday's rise in Brent by 4.09 percent to $108.59 and in U.S. crude by 4.21 percent to $96.31 to the diplomatic impasse and Trump's rejection; the two benchmarks had closed the previous week down by more than 2 percent. Emirates NBD economist Daniel Richards said the rejection had brought the geopolitical premium back to crude by leaving the talks unresolved, while Capital.com analyst Kyle Rodda said the market was pricing in a prolonged impasse. Sources did not record that formal negotiations had resumed, that mediation contacts had ended, or that an agreement was now impossible.

superPackets.body: The Guardian, Daily Maverick, BBC, ABC and Euronews reported that 17 people were killed in Wedela near Johannesburg on Saturday night, and 10 in a separate attack near Cape Town; the initial total for the two attacks was at least 27. Police raised the toll in Wedela to 18 after one person injured there died in hospital; The Straits Times and Euronews thus recorded the total across the two weekend attacks as 28. CBC also reported 28 deaths in these two separate attacks, which occurred hours apart. The figure of 38 used by NPR and ABC was not the weekend total for these two attacks alone, but the total for three separate “mass shootings” over one week; it therefore included a third attack. Sources placed the incidents alongside one another as “mass shootings” and a “wave”; they did not record a common perpetrator, common motive, common organization, or a nationally measured trend.

superPackets.axis: Manchester City’nin Premier League mali kuralları davası, bildirilen komisyon kararı ve koşullu sonuçlar ← Manchester City’nin Premier League mali kurallar davası, bildirilen komisyon kararı ve olası sonuçları.
superPackets.body:
In the verified procedural record, the Premier League process is ongoing and subject to strict confidentiality; the league spokesperson declined to comment on that basis. Manchester City likewise said that significant stages had not been completed; chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak stated that the club remained confident of proving its innocence, but could not share its grounds because of confidentiality.

By contrast, The Athletic reported that City had been found to have breached the rules in 114 of the 115 charges; BBC Sport, citing unnamed sources, also reported that the club had been found at fault on most of the charges. Daily Maverick carried the same reported finding. The independent commission’s written decision has not been published; the Premier League and Manchester City did not confirm the number of breaches reported in the news or the content of the decision.

Possible consequences remained at a separate level. Football finance expert Kieran Maguire assessed that the sanctions would be “significant”; points deductions, relegation or expulsion from the league, the stripping of past titles, and compensation claims by rivals were listed in reports as possible outcomes. The Conversation wrote that the Everton and Nottingham Forest decisions offered limited guidance for the City case, that rivals had no automatic right to compensation, and that a Premier League sanction would not automatically be applied to City Football Group’s other clubs. Guardian commentator Barney Ronay argued that the reported decision had already tarnished City’s period of success; this was commentary, not a published sanction.

Sky Sports wrote that the process could take years because of the scale of the case and possible appeals; other outlets also stated that City was expected to appeal. No source recorded that the commission’s reasoned decision had been officially published, that a sanction had been imposed, that an appeal had been filed, or that any of the possible outcomes had been finalised.

superPackets.axis: Yaklaşan ABD ara seçimleri etrafındaki parti beklentileri, Trump’ın Cumhuriyetçilere etkisi ve oy verme ile seçim çevresi kuralları üzerindeki çatışmalar ← The approaching US midterm cycle: party prospects, Trump’s electoral impact on Republicans, and partisan conflict over voting and redistricting rules.
superPackets.body:
Polls and forecasting models published this week described a favorable midterm environment for Democrats; these were not election results, but current measurements and assessments. In a Wall Street Journal poll, Trump’s approval fell to 37 percent, its lowest level in the outlet’s pre-midterm measurements, while Nate Silver’s aggregation put net approval at minus 23; the same model calculated Democrats’ general-ballot advantage at 9.1 points, their probability of winning the House of Representatives at 91 percent, and their probability of winning the Senate at 69 percent. Charlie Cook described the House shifting to Democrats as “a done deal” and their taking the Senate as “very realistic”; assessments in El País and The Hill likewise attributed voters’ dissatisfaction with Trump and Republican governance to the party’s detriment.

A separate set of records showed the distance some Republicans had put between themselves and Trump. The Atlantic wrote that candidates in Kentucky, Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Iowa and Ohio had removed references to Trump from their campaign websites or diverged from him on issues such as the Iran war, immigration and trade; a Republican operative said these represented not a break with Trump in his entirety, but differences on specific issues. Former Republican Representative Barbara Comstock argued that Trump was “doing everything he can” to help his party lose; Senator Thom Tillis called Trump’s endorsement in the Texas primary a “massive mistake.” By contrast, the White House described Trump as the Republican Party’s “undisputed leader, best messenger and unmatched mobilizer”; records published this week did not provide the measured effect on votes of candidates’ distancing themselves.

The struggle over voting rules and electoral districts proceeded separately from these expectations. The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to use a controversial database to verify voter citizenship; critics questioned the reliability of the data and said U.S. citizens could be mistakenly removed from the rolls. As efforts to restrict voting by mail continued, El País reported early and absentee voting schedules under current state rules; sources did not record the proposed restrictions and procedures currently in force as the same thing. In electoral districts, the Supreme Court prevented Missouri’s new map, described as favoring Republicans, from being used in the November election and left the old map in force; Le Monde wrote that Republicans had succeeded in reshaping districts in other states. No source recorded that this week’s polling movements were caused by citizenship checks, mail-voting rules, or the Missouri map.

superPackets.axis: Aynı aktif Pasifik kasırga döneminde Polo’nun Meksika/Baja California’ya ve Nolo’nun Hawaii’ye yönelik oluşturduğu tehditler ← Hurricane Polo’nun Meksika’nın Pasifik kıyısına, özellikle Baja California’ya, yaklaşması ve oluşturduğu tehdit ⊕ Hurricane Nolo’nun aktif Pasifik kasırga koşulları sırasında Hawaii yakınlarında oluşturduğu tehdit
superPackets.body: CBC, UPI, The Straits Times and Phys.org reported that Polo, weakened to Category 3, was expected to reach the Pacific coast of Baja California Sur on Monday night; forecasts included sustained winds of 100 to 130 kilometres per hour, heavy rain and a risk of flash flooding. In these records, landfall and damage appeared not as events that had yet occurred, but as forecasts and warnings. The Guardian and NPR, meanwhile, placed Nolo on Sunday about 585 kilometres south-southwest of Honolulu, moving away from the Hawaiian Islands at 19 kilometres per hour; Hawaii County Civil Defense reported that a high-wind warning, wind advisory and high-surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening. At that time, Nolo’s maximum sustained winds had reached 115 miles per hour; The Atlantic had earlier reported that the storm had come within about 145 miles of the Big Island and carried a risk of up to 25 inches of rain, flooding and landslides, while UPI reported that it had strengthened to Category 4 on Sunday afternoon and was moving west south of the islands. The Atlantic counted Polo and Nolo among hurricanes simultaneously present in the Pacific and wrote, citing Michael Brennan, that 17 tropical storms had formed in the eastern Pacific at this stage of the season, rather than the average of 12; links involving warm waters and El Niño were also attributed to experts in the same report. The sources did not establish a direct meteorological or causal link between Polo and Nolo; nor did they report Polo’s actual landfall or damage, or confirmed damage or casualties resulting from Nolo’s passage.
